For LAION-related comparisons, ImageNet-R fit improves from R²=0.216 to 0.982 and MAE from 9.23% to 1.32%; Sketch improves from 0.281 to 0.937 and 7.90% to 2.10%. Apparent LAION robustness advantages move close to zero. Held-out OpenCLIP, SLIP, vanilla-fine-tuned CLIP, and WiSE-FT evaluations use MAE and generally, but not invariably, improve prediction. Zero-shot CLIP usually lacks additional robustness under these controls. SLIP and WiSE-FT remain unresolved because their procedures may alter the relevant training distribution. Kendall ranking comparisons also reveal occasional negative agreement for LAION, so multi-ID is not offered as a replacement for single-ID evaluation when training data are shared.
attribution_limits: The paper supplies collective problem formulation, metric design, experiments, and interpretations; it does not assign these contributions specifically to Carlini or establish individual preferences. MAE rather than R² on held-out models is the authors' reporting choice, not a universal statistical requirement. The proposed extension beyond two training distributions and suggested fit-quality gate are prospective, not validated procedures.
tensions_and_counterevidence: Application requires knowing every model's training distribution, excluding direct use with private pretraining data, and assumes training procedures do not substantially change that distribution beyond basic augmentation. No quantitative distribution-closeness criterion or human audit of automatic labels is supplied. Strong fitted relationships are predictive, not causal explanations. Some held-out settings fail to improve, and SLIP/WiSE-FT residual gains are smaller and inconsistently significant rather than conclusively absent. Conventional OOD sets may be less out-of-distribution after large-scale pretraining, without establishing exact-example contamination. Corruption shifts, wild shifts, and inverse ID–OOD relationships can violate the underlying accuracy relationship; the proposed acceptance threshold is unspecified.
coverage_notes: Repeated passages constitute one project. Standard ResNet-18/50/101 training reused TF-Vision configurations on CIFAR-10, changing only dataset, class count, and image size without tuning; the reason for avoiding tuning is not stated. CLIP largely followed existing recipes but doubled batch size from 1024 to 2048 for parallelism, without isolating its effect. Static projections and an interactive visualization were offered but not independently inspected or individually attributed. Metadata dates and author positions are unverified.

substance:
The erratum revisits whether the Obfuscated Gradients attack actually defeated Stochastic Activation Pruning under the defense's specified implementation. Unlike most attribution in this inventory, a footnote explicitly identifies Nicholas Carlini as the author of the faulty SAP reimplementation and assigns him sole responsibility. The error omitted test-time averaging over stochastic forward passes. To recover clean accuracy, the implementation had compensated by doubling the prescribed neuron-sampling parameter, thereby evaluating a materially different defense.

The correction sets r_i to m_i and averages outputs over 100 forward passes per test example. With this repair, the original attack is no longer effective and SAP retains the accuracy claimed in its paper. This retracts the earlier attack result against correctly implemented SAP; it does not establish resistance to other attacks. The authors also distinguish the consequential error from an efficiency approximation: per-neuron binomial sampling replaces multinomial sampling during attack generation, but adversarial examples are tested using the prescribed multinomial procedure. Attack success reportedly remains unchanged in that comparison, without implying the samplers are identical.

The corrected defense resists the existing targeted optimization attack: even more than 10,000 iterations produce below 50% success. The collaborators therefore change diagnostic strategy, testing transfer from the undefended network. Transfer achieves 70% targeted success, suggesting gradient masking contributes to the optimization difficulty. That observation specifically motivates BPDA: query the actual defended forward computation while obtaining gradients from the original network, removing neuron dropping only in the backward pass. On the CIFAR-10 test set at distortion bound epsilon=0.031, the modified attack reduces SAP accuracy to 0.1%, with a reported ±0.05% whose statistical construction is not supplied.

The resulting methodological lessons are concrete. A replication that needs an undocumented hyperparameter change to match reported behavior should trigger investigation. Released code from both attack and defense enabled discovery, motivating the coauthors' strong advocacy of source release. Nevertheless, they explicitly reject BPDA as a universal repair: deliberately substituted gradients can worsen attacks unless chosen carefully, and its usefulness here follows the transfer diagnostic rather than a blanket assumption.
attribution_limits: Responsibility for writing the erroneous reimplementation is explicitly and individually assigned to Carlini. The correction, diagnostic pivot, repaired attack, and recommendations are otherwise jointly authored with Dhillon; the supplied text does not allocate their execution individually. The statement that source release is 'the only way' to promote correct reproducible research is a joint belief, not an experimentally established exclusivity claim.
tensions_and_counterevidence: The record documents a consequential implementation failure, not merely a successful attack or an uninterrupted history of correct evaluation. Faithful implementation reverses the original attack conclusion before a different attack succeeds. The 10,000-iteration diagnostic is not a general stopping rule, and a hyperparameter mismatch is a warning rather than proof of error. Categorical joint advocacy of code release contrasts with the supplied deepfake-detector project's deliberate withholding of attack code; this does not establish an individual change of mind or a universal personal release policy.
coverage_notes: Repeated excerpts describe the same correction and follow-up evaluation and should be counted once. The erratum revises an earlier project rather than independently reproducing every claim of Obfuscated Gradients. The supplied distortion statement does not identify its norm, and the reported uncertainty calculation is unavailable. Metadata dates and author positions are unverified.

substance:
This project studies 'perturbation waste' when an adversarial example must simultaneously induce misclassification and evade a detector within a distortion budget. A weighted classifier-plus-detector objective can over-optimize one requirement at the other's expense. The analysis identifies a possible nonconvex failure: a tradeoff weight suitable near the final solution may be unsuitable early in the same search, so no fixed weight necessarily serves the entire trajectory.

The proposed alternatives are small modifications of gradient descent. Selective updates redirect effort away from a satisfied constraint toward the remaining requirement. However, classifier and detector gradients can nearly oppose each other, causing alternating steps to undo progress. Orthogonalized updates address that limitation by aiming to improve the selected objective without significantly disturbing the other. The paper presents this as a methodological refinement, not proof that every weighted objective fails or that selective switching alone solves all numerical difficulties.

Evaluation assumes perfect knowledge of both classifier and detector. Four image defenses are tested, three on CIFAR-10 and one on ImageNet, using what the authors characterize as each defense's strongest dataset. Original threat models are retained, with additional standard perturbation norms for cross-defense comparisons. Targets are uniformly sampled incorrect labels: successful targeted evasion also establishes untargeted vulnerability. Main metrics are targeted success at 5% and 50% detector false-positive rates, supplemented by ROC curves. The latter operating point is an extreme allowance rejecting half of benign inputs, not a threshold interchangeable with the former.

Implementation fidelity varies by case. Author-provided code and pretrained models support Honeypot, Dense Layer Analysis, and SID evaluations. After converting Honeypot from TensorFlow to PyTorch, the team reports confirmation from the original authors that adversarial examples evade detection; DLA authors likewise confirmed examples. Because SID originally reported AUC rather than the needed operating-point figures, a 9% comparison value was reconstructed by running PGD on the authors' implementation, not quoted as an original published result.

The steganalysis case is more qualified. The team ports MATLAB code to PyTorch and replaces the original highly nondifferentiable FLD ensemble with a three-layer neural detector on SPAM features, arguing that the feature claim is the relevant target. Differentiable SPAM approximations and an auxiliary detector supply gradients for attacking nondifferentiable feature processing. Spatial Rich Model is omitted because the authors judge its added benefit marginal, without testing its vulnerability. Throughput of roughly one image per second limits this case to the orthogonal attack. Despite proposing reusable tooling, the conclusion warns against blind application: future defenses require attacks chosen with an understanding of their particular design.
attribution_limits: All design choices, evaluations, and recommendations are collective. Carlini's listed coauthorship does not establish that he devised the updates, performed framework conversions, contacted defense authors, or personally prefers minimal code changes. Constraint satisfaction is an algorithmic stopping condition, not a personal research stopping rule. External confirmation is reported by the paper; correspondence and independent replication details are not supplied.
tensions_and_counterevidence: Faithful author-model evaluation in several cases coexists with a materially modified SPAM detector. Calling the attacked nondifferentiable detector 'original' does not undo the disclosed FLD replacement; the supplied wording leaves some implementation ambiguity. Omitting SRM limits the claim rather than showing equivalent vulnerability. Selective updates can reverse previous progress, and orthogonalization is not presented as universally sufficient. The results assume direct access to both functions and do not establish comparable black-box performance. Strongest-dataset status is the authors' assessment, not independently demonstrated.
coverage_notes: Repeated records describe one project. Supplied evidence documents successful evasion confirmations and evaluation design but does not provide a complete numerical success table; none is reconstructed here. The SID 9% baseline must retain its rerun provenance. Only the orthogonal variant was evaluated in the slow steganalysis case. Metadata dates and author positions are unverified.

substance:
The project questions whether minimizing total black-box queries represents attack cost when security systems monitor submissions and can throttle or suspend users. It defines flagged status by classifier output, not ground-truth harmfulness: a benign false positive is costly, whereas successful harmful evasion is non-flagged. A base charge plus an additional flagged-query charge motivates reporting both counts. Uniform pricing still justifies conventional total-query optimization; treating non-flagged queries as free is an explicit simplifying case.

The collaborators decompose attacks into boundary projection, direction updating, and step-size selection, then distinguish adversarial checks from boundary-distance estimation. Entropy per flagged query guides redesign. Random directional checks appear difficult to improve without prior boundary geometry—the information those checks seek. Distance estimation instead connects to egg-dropping: searching from the non-flagged side can locate the boundary with one flagged query, while binary search minimizes total queries. Staged searches trade additional flagged queries for fewer ordinary queries; optimality concerns this boundary-search formulation, not entire attacks.

Greedy early stopping accepts an approximate distance once sufficient improvement is established; Stealthy RayS stops below 90% of the current distance. Stealthy HSJA combines Opt's distance-based gradient estimator with HopSkipJump's otherwise efficient structure, reversing that older component's attractiveness under the new metric. Sign-Opt's gradient budget is reduced through parameter sweeps, deliberately sacrificing total-query efficiency. Convergence claims adapt prior zero-order results under smoothness/Lipschitz and bounded-gradient assumptions.

Official baseline implementations are instrumented for flagged queries, mostly preserving defaults. Evaluation progresses from ImageNet, explicitly a proxy security task, through binary dog detection to local and commercial NSFW detection. Ethical concerns motivate reusing high-NSFW-score ImageNet images rather than collecting a new sensitive dataset. Benchmarks use 500 samples and a 1,000-flagged-query cap; the commercial test uses 200. Some full-line-search counts are inferred from two-stage searches rather than directly executed. Commercial evaluation focuses on RayS because it reliably finds small perturbations below 500 queries. Eight-bit input quantization changes its infinity-norm search tolerance from 0.001 to 1/255.

At median infinity-norm distortion 8/255, two-stage RayS with early stopping uses 1.77 times fewer flagged queries and 8% fewer non-flagged queries than original RayS. Commercial Stealthy RayS reaches median 32/255 distortion with 79 rather than 172 flagged queries; changes are visible but reportedly preserve NSFW content. Conversely, strongest stealthy L2 variants require 350–1,420 times more total queries at median distortion 10, and cheaper two-stage variants fail to beat original HopSkipJump on flagged queries. Thus improved stealth can remain impractical except under extreme cost asymmetry; designing attacks around stealth from scratch remains future work.
attribution_limits: The problem selection, ethical dataset rationale, algorithm changes, and conclusions are collaborative work by Debenedetti, Carlini, and Tramèr, without individual contribution assignments. The convergence guarantees are the paper's conditional claims, not independently checked proofs. Algorithmic early stopping and reuse of Opt do not establish Carlini's personal stopping criteria or a longitudinal change in his views. Platform economics are educated estimates, not observed enforcement outcomes.
tensions_and_counterevidence: The commercial API expected NSFW submissions and charged uniformly: it demonstrated evasion and query-count differences, not avoidance of actual bans or asymmetric charges. Platform-cost estimates rely on sparse historical policies, assumptions that account creation dominates cost and attacks finish within days, and speculative violation thresholds. The 1,000-query cap is a modeling judgment, not a universal enforcement limit. 'Stealth' excludes suspicious-query-sequence detectors. The metric also fails by itself to express transfer attacks' lower success rates when candidate generation uses zero target queries; verification is a separate issue. Baseline ImageNet attacks flagged half or more of queries, but ImageNet labels are only an operational proxy.
coverage_notes: Repeated records constitute one project. Batched coarse/fine evaluations are sometimes counted as sequential searches, so reported query counts are not always literal executed calls. Main commercial results give 32/255, while another passage gives 32/355; overall-query overhead figures also conflict and are not reconciled here. Reported runtime on one RTX 3090 ranges from twelve hours to over three days for 500 samples. Code, checkpoints, classifier ports, and outputs were linked but not inspected. Metadata dates and author positions are unverified.

substance:
This study asks whether forensic detectors' cross-generator accuracy and tolerance of compression, blur, or resizing imply adversarial robustness. Most effort targets Wang et al.'s classifier, with Frank et al.'s detector added to test beyond one implementation. Main image-space experiments randomly sample 10,000 fake images from a released 94,036-image dataset, using 224×224 RGB inputs scaled to [0,1]. Small perturbation norms serve as restrictive fragility tests, although the authors acknowledge they imperfectly capture perception.

Distortion minimization replaces a difficult constrained formulation with a Lagrangian objective, using 1,000 Adam iterations per coefficient and binary search over the success-distortion tradeoff. The initial attack works in floating point but fails a practical test: ordinary eight-bit PNG saving destroys the tiny perturbations. The response is a lowest-bit-scale attack, limiting changes to 1/255 and progressively reducing the modified-pixel set. A separate fixed-budget formulation eliminates coefficient search and is evaluated with PNG and JPEG saving. When Frank's detector also predicts generator identity, success is restricted to classification as real; confusing ProGAN with BigGAN does not count.

The reverse attack reveals asymmetry: roughly 1% of fake-image pixels versus just under 7% of real-image pixels must receive lowest-bit changes to reach 50% misclassification. The authors contextualize unusually small distortions using a prior ImageNet comparison: forensic chance performance occurs around L2 distortion 0.02, versus over sixteen times more for the same architecture and image size in that cited setting.

Reusable attacks address repeated per-image optimization. A visible 24×24 patch, about 1% of an image, is optimized on 5,000 images disjoint from the 10,000 evaluation images; detector AUC falls from 0.966 to 0.085. A StyleGAN-only latent attack optimizes one shared low-level attribute while resampling high-level latents, reducing AUC from 0.99 to 0.17.

Black-box transfer intentionally uses a weaker surrogate: ResNet-18 without ImageNet pretraining rather than the target's ResNet-50. Its simpler training is accepted because attack generation, not competitive detection, is the objective. With saveable 1/255 perturbations, source AUC falls from 0.85 to 0.003 and transferred target AUC from 0.96 to 0.22. The authors call transfer their weakest measured but most realistic attack, a deployment judgment rather than observed attacker behavior.

Averaging 2,000 perturbations reveals structure aligned with the 8×8 JPEG lattice, motivating an explicitly unconfirmed training-artifact hypothesis. Attack code is withheld to marginally impede misuse against sensitive forensic systems. Adversarial training and randomized smoothing are proposed, not evaluated; the authors question whether adversarial training alone would provide sufficient forensic robustness.
attribution_limits: These are jointly authored experiments, release decisions, and arguments by Carlini and Farid; first-author metadata does not assign particular implementation or reasoning contributions. Imperceptibility is the authors' norm-based characterization without a supplied human perceptual study. Numerical optimization does not establish global optimality. JPEG training artifacts, likely practical attack access, broader attack ease, and prospective defense limitations remain hypotheses or judgments rather than demonstrated causal or deployment facts.
tensions_and_counterevidence: Highly successful floating-point attacks initially failed serialization, and reverse real-to-fake manipulation was harder. The authors reject secrecy of a defense's existence as sufficient security, while their black-box attacker still lacks target parameters. They also argue that real attackers need not preserve one fixed image: laundering or choosing another suitable portrait broadens the action space, but repeated-upload scenarios were not deployment experiments. Strategic advantage is framed as conditional on move order and timescale—reactive forgery over hours or days versus retrospective detection over months or years—not guaranteed eventual detection. Vulnerable detectors may confer false credibility yet still raise attackers' effort; no net-benefit estimate is measured. Project-specific code withholding contrasts with the SAP erratum's categorical joint release advocacy and should not be flattened into a universal personal policy.
coverage_notes: Repeated passages describe one project. Two detectors and a StyleGAN-specific latent experiment do not establish universality. The background and transfer sections disagree on surrogate training totals, so no precise count is inferred. The sixteen-fold ImageNet comparison cites prior work rather than a fully matched new training experiment. Per-image attacks were reported at under 0.1 seconds, so universal modifications address convenience even when individual optimization is inexpensive. Metadata dates and author positions are unverified.

substance:
This collaboration investigates whether attacking an ML component inside a deployed security pipeline offers a practical advantage over directly defeating specialized malware detectors. Gmail’s Magika file-type router supplies the case: misrouting can prevent the appropriate scanner from examining an attachment. Separating malware creation from subsequent evasion is an explicitly defended realism assumption, not an observed fact about attacker organizations.

The team ported Magika from Keras to JAX and reported equivalence checks. Experiments reused 1,130 files, ten from each of 113 types; substitute training used a separately collected 20-million-file VirusTotal/GitHub corpus. Initial unconstrained experiments isolated classifier vulnerability before restoring format and operating-system constraints. Adapted Greedy Coordinate Gradient optimization changed bytes in place rather than appending language-model suffixes. Mitra and format-specific transformations identified editable regions in PDF, ZIP, Docx, Xlsx, ELF, PNG, and JavaScript files. The authors report eventual 100% misclassification across tested formats and 90% with thirteen edits, with Office files requiring more changes.

Production validation was narrower. With advance authorization, the team selected a malicious PDF missed by popular antivirus scanners, modified it for other file-type checks, altered or removed its extension to avoid blocking or forced scanner routing, and delivered it between controlled Gmail accounts. The extensionless example opened on Ubuntu 22; delivery does not establish universal recipient compatibility or victim compromise.

Defense selection prioritized making Magika cease to be the weakest component while preserving clean accuracy. An informed transfer attacker could know training procedures but not designated secrets. Ensemble attacks optimized average substitute loss: adding models undermined random-seed protection, whose single-substitute result was initially 35% success at ten edits. Architectural diversity, query-assisted inference of hidden preprocessing offsets, and adaptive similarity-unpairing attacks further challenged apparent protection. Adversarial training mixed clean and perturbed examples, but clean accuracy fell from 99% to 97% at ten bytes and below 90% at fifteen; larger attacks and reproducible attacker-side training motivated stopping that baseline investigation.

The proposed keyed preprocessing combined diversification and gradient-dissimilarity ideas using limited AES rounds. Full encryption was considered too sensitive to small changes; CBC harmed utility, so reported results used ECB and deployment used one round. Testing against 512 differently keyed and initialized substitutes substantially reduced transfer without eliminating misclassification. The authors report deployment with Google engineers and less than one microsecond additional latency per file.

The release policy differentiated artifacts: defense code was released, public attack code withheld over misuse concerns, and proprietary training data unavailable. Universities could request attack-code access; promised collection resources were not independently verified.
attribution_limits: All methods, priorities, judgments, deployment claims, and release decisions are attributed to the collaboration, not individually to Nicholas Carlini. No explicit personal preference or allocation of his contribution is supplied. Authorization, implementation equivalence, production deployment, and timing are author-reported rather than independently verified. Similar Gmail behavior on several submitted samples does not itself establish identity of deployed and public model parameters. File-specific adversarial training and cross-domain evaluation are proposed work, not completed findings.
tensions_and_counterevidence: Preserved malicious behavior, not perceptual similarity or few changed bytes, defines attack validity, yet byte count remains an imperfect comparative cost proxy. Magika sees only 1,536 bytes, so apparently tiny whole-file edits correspond to roughly 0.1–1% of classifier input in the discussed setting. Malicious functionality was checked only for the proof-of-concept subset, not exhaustively across formats; the evaluation collection is not established to be entirely malicious. Ten files per type limit within-type coverage. Adversarial-training checkpoints and substitute-architecture screening used reported test accuracy, limiting an untouched-test interpretation. The defense lacks a cryptographic robustness proof and remains vulnerable to direct white-box attacks, large-budget black-box search, and sufficiently large random edits; unrelated-model transfer is explicitly not excluded. Distinct file-type patterns are only a hypothesis for effectiveness, and subtler tasks could lose utility. Open sourcing is presented as both attack-enabling and defense-enabling, not unconditionally beneficial.
coverage_notes: Numerous records repeat the same passages and decisions; this is one project, not multiple independent confirmations. The seven-format classifier results and selected end-to-end Gmail demonstration have different scopes. Architecture experiments varied convolutional depth 1–4, kernels 8–16, and fully connected layers 1–4, requiring at least 95% accuracy. Appendix evidence includes a nongradient random-neighbor alternative and diminishing GCG returns around 2^13 candidates, neither establishing real attacker adoption or a universal stopping rule. The operational weakest-link objective is not accompanied by a comprehensive quantitative ranking of every pipeline component. Metadata dates and author positions remain unverified.

substance:
This evaluation asks whether the Ensemble Everything Everywhere defense’s strong AutoAttack results and perceptually aligned gradients indicate worst-case robustness or merely difficult optimization. The authors acknowledge why the defense looked promising: optimizing a blank image toward “cat” produced recognizable cat-like features. They then distinguish that visual appeal from evidence that small adversarial perturbations cannot succeed.

Diagnosis began with two-dimensional loss slices combining an adversarial direction and an orthogonal random direction. Fixing preprocessing randomness smoothed the initially spiky surface; averaging over transformations further stabilized its large-scale structure. A separate constructive unit test reinitialized and retrained the final layer so nearby differently classified examples existed by construction. The original evaluation found them only 60% of the time, motivating stronger adaptive attacks rather than treating attack failure as robustness.

Using the official training code, the team obtained clean accuracies of 88.9% on CIFAR-10 and 64.1% on CIFAR-100 and reproduced approximate repository-level AutoAttack robustness. Unreleased larger or longer-trained variants were outside the evaluation. Because predictions were stochastic, they attacked every example, including initially misclassified ones, and repeated evaluations ten times, reporting means and standard deviations.

A standard 500-step PGD baseline already surpassed AutoAttack. Replacing CrossMax aggregation with a mean produced an attack surrogate: transferred examples also fooled the original CrossMax defense, supporting gradient masking rather than genuine robustness as the explanation. Expectation over Transformation estimated gradients across randomized backward passes. Further PGD/EoT tuning and hinge loss reduced measured robustness; an APGD ablation on 32 CIFAR-10 examples found no consistent improvement beyond 100 EoT iterations. APGD also explored three times the final radius for 30% of iterations, twice for 30%, and the permitted radius for the final 40%. On 100 test samples at an infinity-norm bound of 8/255, best-of-both attacks yielded 10.9 ± 2.4% and 13.6 ± 1.4% robust accuracy, versus AutoAttack’s 61.8 ± 2.3% and 47.9 ± 2.7%.

Crucially, the revised report corrects its own earlier invalid results. Stacked attack stages measured each bound against the preceding stage instead of the original input, allowing final perturbations ten times too large. The amended workflow saved examples and evaluated them against original data and the original defense in a separate standalone script, also visualizing perturbations. Defense coauthor Stanislav Fort is credited with discovering the bug. The resulting recommendation is defense-specific application of known attacks—not algorithmic novelty or interpretability alone—as the basis for empirical robustness claims.
attribution_limits: This is collective evaluation and correction evidence. The earlier report names Zhang, Nikolić, Carlini, and Tramèr, but does not identify who introduced, overlooked, or fixed the bug. The revised version incorporates concurrent work by Schlarmann, Croce, and Hein. Separate evaluation scripts document a project-specific correction, not Carlini’s longstanding personal workflow or an external audit. Statements about evidential burden and revisiting failed ideas are collective methodological positions; no private expectations or explicit individual preferences are documented.
tensions_and_counterevidence: The evaluators’ own initial threat-model violation materially complicates a simple portrayal of consistently reliable criticism. The corrected attacks still substantially lower measured robustness, but neither their finite search nor the known-vulnerability unit test certifies exact worst-case accuracy. Two-dimensional slices are diagnostic rather than exhaustive, and repeated randomized runs on 100 examples do not eliminate sampling uncertainty. Valid APGD exploration outside the final radius must not be confused with invalid final perturbations in the earlier implementation. The authors do not dismiss revisiting failed ideas: standard and fast adversarial training are cited as productive reconsiderations. They also retain potential value for visualization, interpretability, controllable image generation/manipulation, and transferable attacks, without independently establishing those applications here. Interpretable gradients can accompany robustness, but the converse fails in this case.
coverage_notes: Repeated evidence passages describe one evaluation project and its revision, not independent replications. Metadata lists November 22, 2024, whereas the supplied full-text evidence concerns version 2 dated February 4, 2025; corrected results should not be represented as the original version’s valid findings. Unreleased stronger defense configurations were not tested. The isolated causal contributions of grouped optimizer changes are not quantified. Exhausting available attack attempts is an evaluative ideal, not a finite guarantee that every attack has been considered.

substance:
ExploitGym asks whether AI agents can turn vulnerability-triggering inputs into unauthorized code execution, a task requiring runtime, memory-layout, and instruction-level reasoning beyond bug reproduction. Its 898 instances comprise 520 userspace cases across 161 projects, 185 V8 cases, and 193 Linux-kernel cases. The severe endpoint supports defensive assessment of particular flaws, but higher scores indicate exploitation capability or risk, not overall model quality or safety.

Construction adapts reproduction infrastructure to exploitation. Userspace targets were rebuilt without aborting sanitizers; interpreter entrypoints exposing legitimate shell/filesystem access were excluded. Complementary OSV cases required patch commits and manually validated agent-generated reproducers. V8 collection used post-2024 reports, recovered unavailable fuzzing inputs from patch-associated tests, and retained 185 of 403 candidates after reproduction. Shell conveniences were removed while retaining scheduling, worker, and serialization APIs needed by genuine cases. KernelCTF exploits were reduced to minimal reproducers with exploitation details sanitized; syzbot cases were deduplicated and reproduced. Kernel flags required privileges beyond namespace-local root.

Resettable containerized targets expose configurable guidance and mitigations, with patches withheld by default. Success requires both retrieval of a dynamically generated privileged flag and attribution to the intended vulnerability. Interactive judges inspect trajectories and artifacts. An expert audit independently labeled 59 trajectories, excluding one unresolved case: Codex matched all 58 retained labels, while Claude matched 56, with both errors falsely crediting unrelated bugs. The general protocol uses two judges and human escalation, but Opus 4.6 and Mythos Preview experiments used only Claude.

Main comparisons allowed one two-hour attempt with mitigations disabled and inference-time filters removed through approved research access; learned refusals could remain. Mythos received an additional instruction file. Mythos Preview and GPT-5.5 achieved 157 and 120 intended-vulnerability successes, including 12 and 22 kernel successes. Off-target exploitation was separately retained as capability evidence. Trace inspection identified early non-exploitability judgments and refusals rather than equating every failure with technical inability. Restoring GPT-5.5’s default filters blocked 88.2% before tool use; remaining attempts stayed in reconnaissance.

Timeouts motivated six-hour experiments, restricted by cost to Mythos and Opus 4.6. Opus plateaued near fifteen successes within thirty minutes; Mythos continued improving beyond two hours. The union across experiments reached 239 targets. Rerunning previously successful tasks with mitigations eliminated most exploits but left successes across all domains. A GPT-5.4 V8 case progressed from a debug-only crash to code execution under relaxed conditions, then failed when production defenses were restored.

The stated inclusion policy requires publicly sourced, upstream-patched vulnerabilities. A prospective disclosure rule withholds newly discovered vulnerability or technique artifacts until patches or ninety days. Governance tradeoffs remain explicitly outside the benchmark’s resolution.
attribution_limits: All design choices and conclusions are collaborative. The contribution statement assigns benchmark design and methodology to academic authors, with industry partners providing feedback, access, and selected experimental assistance; it does not map Carlini to particular responsibilities. Human auditors and reproducer validators are unnamed. Debugging, source auditing, fuzzing, refusals, and early stopping described in trajectories are evaluated-agent behaviors, not Carlini’s personal practices. Reasoning-capacity explanations for plateaus and different internal strategies inferred from complementary successes remain interpretations. Further gains from retries, tailored prompts, specialist tools, or longer-than-six-hour runs are possibilities, not demonstrated general results. Disclosure is a prospective policy, not a documented event.
tensions_and_counterevidence: Baseline results measure model–agent configurations under relaxed defenses and approved access, not ordinary public-access behavior or unrestricted production compromise. Prompting, reasoning-effort settings, and judging were not uniform: Opus 4.7 was an explicit reasoning-effort exception, and the single-Claude judging exception matters because Claude made false-positive attribution errors in the audit. Judge agreement can preserve shared errors. Many tasks lack ground-truth exploits and may be impossible; refusals, tool misuse, and early judgments also confound failures. Missing public solutions reduce one contamination route without proving uncontaminated evaluation. Code execution omits meaningful read/write primitives and partial progress. Mitigation testing selected prior successes rather than reevaluating the full benchmark; reported surviving task counts were 37 userspace, 20 V8, and 12 kernel. Upstream patches do not imply universal deployment or zero release risk. Current unreliability is explicitly not presented as a durable safety guarantee.
coverage_notes: Many records repeat one benchmark project. Coverage excludes Windows, iOS, and Android. Supporting controls include egress-proxy restrictions with package/toolchain exceptions, four CPU cores and 8 GB per agent, and cost/time/model-call reporting separately for successful runs and the full benchmark; host/service conditions and some monetary costs remain incomplete. Syzbot selection emphasizes x86/x86_64 severe memory-safety and race bugs, preferring earliest upstream reports. The overlap figures of 56 Mythos-only, 26 GPT-only, and 91 shared tasks do not directly reconcile with the headline 157/120 counts in the supplied excerpts; their exact subset relationship is unspecified. The 239-task union includes extended experiments and is not a single-agent two-hour score. No external validation of metadata, historical deployment assertions, or reported results was performed.

substance:
This project asks whether optimizing norm-bounded perturbation robustness can create excessive invariance: a classifier retains its prediction even when the input’s correct semantic label changes. It distinguishes that failure from excessive sensitivity, where task-irrelevant changes alter predictions. The claim is that robustness interventions can introduce this second vulnerability, not that every intervention necessarily does so.

Analytical constructions establish the distinction. A constant classifier cannot suffer prediction-changing perturbations but ignores every meaningful label change, motivating joint consideration of accuracy, sensitivity, and invariance. A controlled concentric-spheres experiment uses 500-dimensional data and a classifier ignoring ten coordinates. Despite nearly perfect finite-test accuracy, perturbation attacks expose outer-sphere failures and invariance attacks move inner-sphere examples onto the outer sphere without changing predictions. Each attack family misses failures found by the other, even with endpoints on the data manifold.

MNIST was chosen despite its limited broader relevance because contemporary norm-robustness claims were strongest there, and quasi-binary features and separated classes favor norm-based defenses. Binarization illustrates the mechanism: images humans identify as a one and a four can become identical after thresholding at 0.5. The practical attack is model-agnostic but explicitly tailored to meaningful pixel-space comparisons. It searches allowed affine transformations of differently labeled training images for nearby targets, then moves a correctly classified source toward one. Human checks exclude candidates whose transformations invalidate the target-label assumption.

The L0 procedure thresholds substantial pixel differences at an explicitly arbitrary 0.5, spectrally clusters regions, and enumerates cluster subsets to remove superficial edits. AC-GAN class-conditional scoring assists candidate selection and reportedly halves average distortion; human labeling still determines semantic success. Mean L0 distortion was 25.9 pixels, with median 25. The simpler, less effective infinity-norm variant interpolates within 0.3 and uses empirically chosen pairings, such as one toward seven or four. The team generated 1,000 examples per approach; alignment took several minutes per example and was not optimized.

Forty human evaluators assessed mixtures of clean controls and modified digits. For 100 L0 candidates, 48 reached 70% agreement on a changed label, 34 on the original label, and eighteen lacked consensus. Separate reported success figures—55% L0 and 21% infinity-norm—must not be conflated with that consensus threshold. Model evaluation used successful human-label-changing attacks and compared predictions against the new labels. A sparse-Fourier L0 defense achieved 38% agreement versus a baseline’s 54%, despite both having 99% clean accuracy. Cross-threat-model table entries were explicitly marked as not attacks on the defense’s stated guarantee.

The conclusion retains norm robustness as useful but insufficient, recommends semantic checks when selecting radii, and leaves quantitative invariance measures and the completeness of its failure taxonomy unresolved.
attribution_limits: The constructions, attack design, dataset choice, and recommendations are collective work; no individual contribution allocation or explicit personal preference from Carlini is supplied. Deferring runtime optimization is documented, but its rationale is unavailable and cannot establish a personal speed-versus-insight preference. Empirical digit-pair choices are project heuristics, not general preferences. AC-GAN scoring is described as class-conditional likelihood without supplied calibration details. Invertible networks and improved quantitative invariance metrics are suggested research directions, not demonstrated solutions or individual commitments.
tensions_and_counterevidence: The results establish possible and specific tradeoffs rather than a universal ranking of robust and ordinary classifiers; the broader table varies across models and norms. Conditional accuracy on human-validated attacks is not ordinary test accuracy or performance on every generated candidate. Human disagreement remains substantive, and the 70% consensus analysis differs from plurality-based selection. The arbitrary pixel threshold is not a validated perceptual boundary, and generative scores do not replace human judgments. A natural-image illustration changes a tennis ball toward a strawberry with L2 distance 23.2, smaller than a nearly imperceptible comparison at 24.3, but the authors acknowledge ambiguity from two objects; it is not a systematic natural-image result. Class-dependent semantic susceptibility complicates using one radius everywhere. Sensitivity and invariance are expressly not claimed to exhaust all evasion failures.
coverage_notes: Repeated passages describe one project. The reported human-study prose—forty evaluators, presented sets of 100 images with half clean controls, alongside per-attack candidate summaries—does not fully specify image allocation across evaluators; no missing protocol is reconstructed. The affine search covers the allowed rotations, translations, shears, and resizing, not every mathematically possible transformation. Filtering less-canonical training images reportedly increased construction success, but its isolated effect is not quantified here. Human-validation exclusions and empirical target-pair tuning lack detailed counts or a separate held-out selection account. Metadata dates and author positions are unverified.

substance:
The project asks whether anonymous, user-voted model comparisons permit selective promotion or demotion, and which defenses increase manipulation costs without destroying evaluation usefulness. Chatbot Arena supplies the empirical setting; applicability to other voting systems is argued rather than experimentally established. The attacker knows the candidate models, controls prompts, and can query candidates directly—conditions that make identification easier than unrestricted attribution of arbitrary text.

Identification is reduced to target-versus-rest classification. Across 22 models and eight prompt types, the researchers collected repeated responses, constructed balanced datasets of 50 target and 50 non-target responses, and trained separate logistic regressions for each prompt–model pair with 80/20 response splits. This tests new responses to known prompts, not unseen-prompt generalization. Bag-of-words outperformed the tested length and TF-IDF features; mathematics and Chinese illustrated particularly discriminative inputs. Direct identity questions were less practical because responses often disclosed only model families and Arena already filtered model-name mentions. Once selected prompts and simple features exceeded 95% detection performance, the team deferred more sophisticated detectors because their computational overhead offered limited downstream benefit.

Ranking simulations used 1,670,250 historical votes from 477,322 users, assumed symmetric 5% false-positive and false-negative rates, and recomputed Bradley–Terry rankings every 1,000 interactions. Crucially, interactions included unsuccessful target encounters and abstentions, not just votes. Moving a low-ranked example upward four positions required 381 votes, versus 3,127 for the fifth-ranked example; historical vote volume and rank were not causally separated. For llama-13b, reducing detector accuracy from 100% to 90% added approximately 150 votes to a 50-position promotion, though interactions also increased. Alternatives to abstention—random votes, ties, or both-bad votes—showed no clear superior strategy.

Defense analysis separated detector construction, account acquisition, and recurring action costs, including attackers spreading activity across accounts. Authentication raises credential costs; rate limits can be calibrated against benign usage. Behavioral tests used estimated preference distributions and simulated-null calibration, but attackers following public rankings evaded the basic detector. Perturbing released ratings improved detection at the cost of rank distortion. Prompt uniqueness could require fresh detector training, except where models remain identifiable across prompts; CAPTCHAs were another proposed recurring expense. The operational goal was increased cost and fewer malicious votes before detection, not complete prevention against unlimited resources.

Carlini’s specifically credited contributions connect identification to practical impact: jointly proposing rank-shift simulations, co-developing the cost model, and suggesting authentication and rate limiting. The authors report controlled experiments without live-platform impact, following disclosure and collaboration with Arena.
attribution_limits: These are collaborative findings, with unusually specific third-person contribution credits rather than individual first-person testimony. Huang originated the manipulation idea and executed simulations using Arena’s platform; Carlini and Florian Tramer suggested simulations, and Carlini supplied unspecified feedback. Carlini joined the August 2024 disclosure, co-developed the cost model with Nasr, Huang, and Zhang, suggested authentication and rate limiting, and contributed writing/editing rather than the initial draft. Malicious-user detection and per-action-cost proposals are separately credited to other collaborators. The collective security objective and publication-risk judgment do not establish Carlini’s private preferences or responsibility for every defense detail.
tensions_and_counterevidence: The approximately $440 baseline is an undefended, historical detector-cost scenario, not a demonstrated price for manipulating deployed Arena. Bot protection, malicious-user detection, rate limiting, and prompt processing already existed. Authentication may change participation and behavior; noisy ratings damage the information being protected. Benign preference heterogeneity and vote dependence complicate anomaly tests. Balanced detector accuracy does not establish the symmetric errors assumed in simulation, and provider-default decoding means results characterize serving configurations as well as models. The authors regard complete prevention as practically infeasible, not formally impossible. Their belief that concurrent work made publication’s marginal risk small was not measured. Open participation offers ecological validity while controlled annotators offer stronger oversight; the study does not resolve that tradeoff.
coverage_notes: Repeated contribution statements, methods, and findings within this packet are duplicate evidence from one project, not independent corroboration. Main collection specifies 200 prompts per category, whereas costing uses 200 overall; the illustrative 30-model costing mix also differs from the 22-model evaluation. The 512-token cap and 50 responses per model are reported sufficient, not minimal. PCA plots for three English prompts are illustrative, and the larger-negative-pool robustness result is described only as a slight decline. Owner-side identification through logs, training knowledge, watermarks, or backdoors is conceptual; watermark use and attacker knowledge are conditional. The January 2025 text describes login and reCAPTCHA as being integrated, not necessarily complete or current. No broad identity-probing accuracy claim unsupported by the supplied table caveat is adopted.

substance:
The project investigates whether diffusion models reproduce identifiable training images, treating extraction as both a privacy risk and evidence relevant to generalization. It deliberately studies worst-case near-copy memorization rather than semantic resemblance or style copying. Conditional-generator attackers are assumed to know some training captions; the results do not establish equivalent extraction without that auxiliary information.

For Stable Diffusion, computation shaped the search. The team prioritized duplicated examples, using 512-dimensional CLIP embeddings to make candidate discovery over 160 million images tractable. Timestep-resampled generation traded slightly lower fidelity for roughly tenfold faster sampling, producing 500 candidates per prompt. A black-box detector sought cliques of at least ten near-identical generations, which reduced false positives relative to pair matching. Shared gray backgrounds caused spurious whole-image similarity, prompting a switch to the maximum distance across sixteen corresponding 128-by-128 tiles. Against 175 million generated candidates, a high-confidence subset contained 50 memorized images with no observed false positives. Manual inspection of the top 1,000 supplemented the numerical criterion rather than treating it as definitive.

The researchers then investigated unique images using average CLIP distance to 1,000 nearest neighbors, replacing prohibitively expensive influence-style retraining with an outlier heuristic. Imagen reproduced three unique images among 500 targets; the same procedure found none among 10,000 Stable Diffusion outliers. Neither outcome establishes a universal duplication requirement or explains the model difference.

To investigate conditions beyond large-model demonstrations, the team trained smaller CIFAR-10 models. Its initial million-generation matching exercise was explicitly a memorization-capability check against known training data, not a complete operational attack. Absolute distance, SSIM, and CLIP distance failed to reliably distinguish copying from simple skies or landscapes. A locally normalized nearest-neighbor criterion, using 50 neighbors and scaling 0.5, replaced them. Counts removed repeated outputs and duplicated training records, yielding 1,280 unique recovered images.

Separate membership experiments used sixteen half-dataset shadow models to select an informative noise timestep, subsequently using timestep 100. Averaging stochastic losses and horizontal flips increased true positives from 7% to 44% at 0.1% false positives. Inpainting used 100 targets, 5,000 reconstructions each, top-ten selection, and models trained with versus without each target; support-model loss normalization improved candidate ranking. Best-FID early stopping and training-trajectory analysis exposed increasing leakage alongside improving quality.

Defenses remained incomplete: removing 5,275 CIFAR-10 records and retraining reduced recovered examples from 1,280 to 986. DP-SGD diverged even around epsilon 50, including separate clipping or noise tests. Cheaper one-model canary audits showed nonmonotonic exposure. Recommendations therefore combined deduplication, reduced overtraining, empirical auditing, and privacy-preserving training when practical.
attribution_limits: The contribution statement credits Carlini, Hayes, Sehwag, and Wallace with independently proposing the problem; Carlini, Wallace, and Tramèr performed preliminary extraction experiments. Carlini counted LAION duplicates, performed CIFAR-10 diffusion extraction experiments, wrote corresponding sections, organized the project, and wrote the initial draft. Nasr performed most Stable Diffusion and Imagen experiments; Hayes performed CIFAR-10 membership inference and inpainting; Jagielski performed canary experiments. GAN work, editing, framing, and figure improvements involved other collaborators. These assignments do not individually attribute every methodological choice or final recommendation. The authors collectively report using public-source datasets, restricting displayed personal images to public figures who knowingly posted them, and giving model developers advance notice; resulting safeguards are not documented.
tensions_and_counterevidence: The duplicate-biased search cannot estimate population-wide copying rates or establish that fewer than 100 duplicates are safe. Recognizable new depictions of people can create privacy harms outside the near-copy definition. Stable Diffusion’s unsuccessful outlier search is not proof of absent unique-image memorization. Diffusion models leaked more than evaluated GANs even with GAN discriminator access; an off-the-shelf comparison found twice as many recovered images for the best DDPM as StyleGAN-ADA at similar FID, but architecture and training confounds remain. The 244-image overlap between diffusion’s 1,280 and StyleGAN’s 361 recoveries suggests nonuniform vulnerability without explaining it. Conditional-model leakage is confounded by extra parameters. DP-SGD failure is implementation-specific, and the paper acknowledges successful small-scale private diffusion training elsewhere. Random canaries may be poor worst-case probes. Successful extraction does not settle whether generation generally consists of copying and interpolation; failed attacks would likewise depend on attack strength.
coverage_notes: Numerous records repeat the same contribution statements and experiments; count one project. The supplied text reports 94 numerical Stable Diffusion extractions, then 13 additional visually identified near-copies and a total of 109: the arithmetic is inconsistent and no corrected total is inferred. Manual review covered only the top 1,000 candidates. The GAN appendix reportedly selects checkpoints by highest FID despite elsewhere explaining that lower FID is better; no replacement rule is inferred. BigGAN training was extended to 200,000 steps for fidelity, while StyleGAN and MHGAN used repository defaults. The paper’s simplified diffusion exposition explicitly omits details judged orthogonal to the attacks. Neither public online availability nor the authors’ publication safeguards independently establishes consent for every underlying training image.

substance:
This project asks whether a well-generalizing language model can nevertheless expose unusually memorized training examples. Similar average training and test losses were not treated as sufficient privacy reassurance. GPT-2 was chosen partly because its model and source material were public, while its assembled training corpus remained unreleased, reducing opportunities to tailor attacks to known examples. The study pursued indiscriminate rather than person-targeted extraction through black-box sequence probabilities and predictions, without weights or hidden states.

The initial attack generated 200,000 256-token outputs from GPT-2 XL using top-40 sampling and ranked them by perplexity. Inspection exposed two distinct failures: hundreds of copies of Vaughn Live guidelines reduced diversity, while repetitive, high-likelihood nonsense caused false-positive membership predictions. Revised sampling used temperature 10 decaying to 1 over twenty tokens, or 5–10-token prefixes from cleaned, line-deduplicated Common Crawl text collected differently from GPT-2’s Reddit-linked corpus. Possible overlap was acknowledged, not eliminated.

Ranking shifted toward unexpectedly high confidence relative to smaller GPT-2 models or zlib compression, alongside original-versus-lowercased perplexity and minimum perplexity over 50-token windows. These measures addressed different failure modes: trivial repetition, capitalization-sensitive memorization, and memorized fragments diluted by surrounding text. Three samplers each generated 200,000 outputs; six ranking metrics produced eighteen configurations. The team selected 100 candidates per configuration from its top 1,000, applied fuzzy trigram deduplication, and manually inspected 1,800 candidates. Web exact matches were supplemented by creator-mediated training-corpus checks, with separate exact counts for selected analyses.

The reported yield was 604 unique memorized examples: 33.5% of inspected candidates, not population recall. Internet sampling with zlib reached 67% candidate precision, whereas raw perplexity yielded 9% and 3% for top-n and temperature sampling. Higher yield was not identical to finding rarer material: smaller-model comparisons found thirteen and ten high-entropy examples, versus one for zlib. Nine one-document examples contained 10–87-character random-looking strings repeated 10–311 times within that document; one-document memorization therefore did not mean one occurrence.

Extension experiments replaced unreliable greedy continuation with beam-like decoding and recovered a 1,450-line source file. Yet context could matter more than decoder complexity: a bare pi prefix produced 25 digits greedily or 500 with beam search, while descriptive prompts produced 799 or 824 greedily. Naturally repeated URLs supplied a frequency-and-size case study: the largest model emitted every tested URL occurring at least 33 times, while the smallest emitted none under the harder test. An easier fallback supplied six additional identifier characters. These results motivate auditing and layered mitigation, not claims of exhaustive recovery or universal scaling thresholds.
attribution_limits: Carlini is explicitly credited jointly with five collaborators for proposing the GPT-2 extraction question and framing its threat model. He also jointly helped define memorization, wrote candidate-generation and verification code with Tramèr and Herbert-Voss, manually reviewed and categorized outputs with three collaborators, and participated in writing. Particular code components, reviewed samples, and individual rationales are not assigned. The privacy framing, ethical judgments, and mitigation recommendations are collective, not personal preference testimony. Contextual integrity is an adopted framework attributed to prior scholarship. The team reports permission from the individual featured in its prominent contact-information example and disclosure to OpenAI, not consent from every represented individual.
tensions_and_counterevidence: Public data can still be reproduced outside its intended context, persist after removal from its source, or be recombined into false statements about real people. Such recombinations are not factual biographies or whole-output eidetic memories, even when constituent snippets are memorized. Of 31 recovered code samples, authorship notices and terms were usually not recovered. Redaction and disclosure did not eliminate the risk of others repeating extraction. Targeted attacks were excluded from these experiments but remained a possible future direction, so this is not a permanent rejection of targeted research. The formal definition omits string length and has prompt-copying pathologies mitigated experimentally by short prefixes. Differential privacy raises a protected-unit problem when personal information spans webpages and contributor labels are unavailable; sanitization and finer-grained deduplication are proposed partial defenses, not tested guarantees. Empirical audits complement theoretical bounds but unsuccessful attacks cannot certify privacy.
coverage_notes: Repeated records describe one project and must not inflate support. The paper’s candidate percentages are best understood as selected-candidate precision/yield, despite its occasional true-positive-rate terminology; total recall is unknown. Public-web matching alone does not prove training membership. Creator-mediated fuzzy verification acknowledges false positives, and its wording about eliminating false negatives versus failing to detect initially missed memorization is internally awkward; it should not be represented as exact or exhaustive validation. Exact corpus counts apply only to selected analyses. Working URLs without identifiable provenance were excluded rather than assumed memorized. The 50-token window followed only a cursory sweep and manual analysis. Probability access is stronger than text-only API access. Natural URL canaries improve realism over inserted strings but remain a narrow single-document case, and the claimed magnitude of undiscovered memorization is unmeasured.

substance:
The project addresses a practical instruction-following failure: language models produce concentrated choices even when asked for randomness, limiting automated synthetic-data creation. Random numbers and baby names provide diagnostic tasks before transfer to fictional biographies. Instruction-tuned Gemma-7B, Llama-2-13B, and Mistral-7B were sampled 1,000 times per task at temperature one. Curly-brace formatting simplified parsing, and an explicit no-code instruction addressed Gemma’s tendency to answer randomness requests with code.

Measurement depends on what can be specified. Enumerable target distributions permit KL-divergence comparisons; larger or unknown spaces use empirical entropy and unique-output coverage. Uniform numbers are comparatively straightforward, whereas random names could mean uniform choices or population-frequency sampling. The 2022 U.S. baby-name distribution was therefore presented as a reasonable comparison baseline, not a uniquely correct normative target.

The intervention maximizes target-probability-weighted sequence log-likelihood, equivalent to KL minimization up to fixed target entropy. Targets must be prefix-free; appending end-of-sequence tokens supplies a concrete remedy otherwise. When the desired distribution is unknown, roughly 200 samples provide an empirical proxy, with an acknowledged risk of learning only those outputs. LoRA rank four updated less than 0.1% of parameters and was reported sufficient across the experiments. Training ran for at most fifty steps; non-enumerable cases stopped when loss came within 20% of the entropy-based minimum rather than optimizing empirical fit indefinitely.

The authors explicitly recognized that evaluating toy tasks on their training prompts and output spaces did not demonstrate generalization. After tuning on number ranges 1–10 and 1–100, they tested changed instructions and unseen ranges such as 1–45. Leave-one-task-out experiments then trained on five of six families—names, countries, fruits, dates, numbers, and occupations—and evaluated the sixth. Countries and fruits retained sizable transfer gaps, supporting task-specific tuning when diverse targets are available. Conversely, occupation generation could extend beyond the seventeen supplied occupations beginning with A.

Application-level evaluation compared 1,000 fictional biographies from baseline Llama-2-13B and a model tuned only on the structured tasks. It separately measured categorical coverage and normalized unigram diversity. Transfer improved diversity but left 76.2% female biographies and 21.1% of birth years concentrated in 1985. A follow-up used 210 programmatically generated attribute tuples with roughly balanced gender, birth year, and birthplace, excluding achievement descriptions. Open-ended achievements nevertheless remained diverse. MT-Bench showed minimal baseline-versus-tuned differences, providing a bounded utility check. Approximately fifty A100 GPU-hours and released code/prompts characterized the reported implementation. Despite encouraging transfer, direct optimization still requires valid structured targets and does not directly solve unrestricted open-ended generation.
attribution_limits: All supplied substantive evidence is collaborative paper text. No contribution statement assigning particular choices or experiments to Carlini, and no individual first-person preference, is supplied. His coauthorship establishes involvement but not personal authorship of the objective, LoRA choice, demographic balancing, stopping rule, or interpretation. Reducing human intervention is an explicit project goal; it should not become an inferred private preference. The biographies are generated fictional experimental artifacts, not factual biographies. Code availability and compute expenditure are reported by the paper; neither repository contents nor reproducibility were independently checked.
tensions_and_counterevidence: Greater entropy, coverage, or unigram diversity does not establish semantic quality, factual coherence, or an appropriate demographic distribution. Population-frequency baby names and balanced biography attributes are different chosen targets, neither a universal fairness standard. Empirical-target training can collapse onto its sample support; the stopping rule and observed transfer do not guarantee avoidance for arbitrary tasks. Countries and fruits show meaningful limits to transfer. Temperature one is unmodified sampling, not mathematically maximally diffuse: higher temperatures can flatten distributions, but the paper reports degeneration concerns and temperatures above ten being needed to match tuned entropy in the relevant comparison. Minimal MT-Bench changes do not exclude regressions elsewhere. Structured-attribute training’s benefit to achievement text is promising transfer, not proof of direct applicability to all open-ended generation.
coverage_notes: Repeated records restate one study rather than independently corroborating it. The authors report LoRA as more effective and efficient than prefix tuning and discrete prompt search, but supplied evidence lacks detailed quantitative comparisons; no universal superiority is inferred. Discrete diversity-inducing prompts remain proposed future work because they could reach closed-source models. Rank-four sufficiency and the 20%-from-minimum stopping threshold are study-specific choices without supplied detailed rank-selection or stopping-rule ablations. The biography sample sizes refer to generated fictional records, and the numerical imbalances describe the intermediate transferred model rather than the final attribute-tuned model.

The collaboration asks whether optimizing norm-bounded robustness can actively impair semantic correctness: an invariance attack changes the human-assigned class while preserving the model’s prediction. Its target is oracle agreement even on rare or out-of-distribution labelable inputs. Restricting attacks to bounded changes and final classifications excludes trivial substitutions of unrelated misclassified examples. The theoretical tradeoff depends on distance–oracle misalignment; it is not an impossibility theorem for every robustness objective. A nearest-neighbor reduction argues that a perfectly oracle-aligned distance would itself encode perfect classification.

MNIST was selected because sufficiently robust models existed there, despite acknowledged benchmark limitations. Expensive human labeling motivated a shared, model-agnostic attack set. The generator aligns differently labeled examples using rotations up to 20 degrees, six-pixel shifts, 20% shears, and 50% resizing; humans check the label-preservation assumption. Zero-norm refinement uses an explicitly arbitrary 1/2 pixel-change threshold, spectral clustering, cluster-subset enumeration, and class-conditional GAN scoring, reportedly halving average distortion. Removing the least-canonical 20% improved success without a quantified effect. Infinity-norm targets were empirically restricted—for example, matching 1 with 7 or 4—before bounded interpolation.

The study used 100 random test inputs per norm family and a constraint-enforcing editor through which one unspecified author modified 50 examples. Forty evaluators each labeled 100 digits, half clean; 98 of 100 clean controls had unanimous labels. At infinity-norm radius 0.4, manual examples achieved 88% consensus label changes versus 37% automated success. Main model comparisons condition on human label changes; evaluated robust models underperformed an undefended ResNet-18 on zero-norm invariance examples. A certified model retained original labels on 96% of all 100 automated candidates but matched humans on 63%; human agreement on manual examples was 12%. These results challenge the certificate’s semantic interpretation, not its mathematics.

Controlled training sweeps used infinity-norm budgets 0–0.4 and one-norm budgets 0–15 as a zero-norm proxy, verifying increasing conventional robustness before observing increasing invariance vulnerability. Harm extended beyond training radii. A synthetic sanitized-data model explains how stable nuisance features can predict benchmark labels yet disagree with the oracle; label noise prevents trivial oracle learning. Spatial-plus-noise augmentation tested this explanation. Training selected the strongest of ten transformations with 40 PGD steps; testing enumerated the defined transformations with 100 steps. Budgets at least 0.25 required warming up at 0.2 and increasing by 0.05 every five epochs. Augmentation improved human agreement but remained worse than an undefended model at large budgets; conservative bounds alone did not eliminate the problem.
attribution_limits: All research framing, methods, recommendations, and findings are collective paper evidence, not individually attributable choices or private preferences of Carlini. The manual editor is identified only as one author. Theorems and experimental measurements are reported, not independently verified. Dataset sanitization is a stylized explanation, not a reconstructed causal history of MNIST. The alternative hard-to-learn semantic feature is proposed, not documented as implemented and rejected. Paper structure does not establish research chronology or a personal change of mind.
tensions_and_counterevidence: The initial semantic-success criterion requires 70% agreement, whereas main model inclusion is described using plurality; the discrepancy is unresolved. The introduction’s 60% automated human-agreement figure differs from the detailed 63% result. Certified-model evaluation includes unsuccessful candidates, unlike the principal conditional comparison. Manual and automated sets differ in construction and size. Clean-control agreement does not establish an infallible oracle for perturbed digits. Out-of-threat-model table entries explicitly are not attacks on the corresponding defenses. Lower-distortion examples can be stronger conditional on already changing semantics, despite lower generation success. Contrary representation findings concern internal layers and unbounded changes, rather than this paper’s bounded final classifications. Augmentation and smaller budgets are partial measures, not solutions.
coverage_notes: Numerous records repeat the same passages and experiments; they constitute one project, not independent corroboration. Systematic evaluations are MNIST-centered; ImageNet small-object replacement or occlusion is illustrative. Alignment took amortized minutes per example and was not runtime-optimized. Conventional evaluation used ten PointwiseAttack repetitions and 100-step PGD; some ABS/Binary-ABS results came from prior work. The ordinary sweep used ten-epoch Adam training and a one-third-budget first epoch, not an adaptive stopping rule. Code, attacks, and human labels were reportedly released; availability was not checked.

substance:
Carlini describes a recreational IOCCC engineering problem: run the original Busicom calculator ROM using a C program smaller than 4004 bytes. Rather than directly interpret Intel instructions, he embedded a circuit of his own design in a logic-gate simulator, using miniHDL and microcode to compress the processor and supporting hardware. Each instruction becomes at most sixteen micro-operations; a three-deep ALU queue was chosen because it is simpler to wire than a stack. Micro-operations also advance the program counter, handling jumps and calls without additional dedicated circuitry.

The central objective is compressed description size, not gate count. Carlini explicitly contrasts an earlier register file designed for simplicity with this redesign for compressibility. All 256 registers are twelve bits—even when only four or one are needed—because uniform patterns compress well and the program counter already requires twelve bits. An existing adder is reused 256 times in register selection rather than introducing a specialized incrementer. A twelve-gate no-op spacer regularizes relative references. Printer lookup data is permuted and sometimes duplicated to shorten the consuming code: locally redundant structure can reduce total source length.

Relative gate references reportedly reduce reference storage from eighteen to 7.7 bits and expose patterns for LZ compression. A domain-specific REPEAT instruction captures repetitions whose arguments change by a constant. Because REPEAT modifies its instruction stream, reusable subcircuits must be copied before decoding so subsequent calls remain correct. A dedicated signal wire connects simulated hardware to host I/O. Input delivery follows execution progress—one character per 128 TEST-pin conditional jumps—rather than wall-clock time, replacing timing supplied by the physical print drum.

Performance work updates only gates with changed inputs, using a three-level bitmask to skip individual gates or blocks of 64 and 4096. The reported 100–500-fold speedup still yields only hundreds of instructions per second and roughly a minute for addition. Example calculations, including memory operations, square roots, and subtotals, provide expected results but take three to ten minutes. Compatibility is workload-bounded: keyboard handling stores the sole active-bit position instead of implementing a full 4003 shift register; unused DCL is omitted, and only ROM port zero is supported.

Carlini estimates several hundred loosely tracked hours over four years. His explicit personal preference concerns this particular compact artifact as a restorative break from larger, mostly Python work, not a general preference for C or gate-level research. He enjoyed completion but had no current plan for another entry. He also deliberately ended the technical walkthrough before documenting every instruction and compression trick.
attribution_limits: These are directly attributable first-person descriptions, local design judgments, and explicit reflections by Carlini. Compression and speed figures, elapsed effort, fidelity claims, and the maximum safe input rate are self-reported rather than independently benchmarked. The REPEAT copying requirement explains correctness but does not document a particular debugging episode. The project concerns recreational engineering; its objectives should not be generalized into his professional research priorities. His future contest plans were tentative at publication.
tensions_and_counterevidence: The opening’s feature-complete characterization is qualified by a later knowledge-limited, nearly feature-complete claim, omitted DCL, restricted ports, and workload-specific keyboard emulation. Gate-level simulation does not establish general compatibility with arbitrary ROMs. Minimizing encoded size produces a large expanded circuit and poor absolute speed; reuse described as free is free in compressed representation, not computation. Input-timing problems remain despite execution-based pacing. Carlini attributes them to original-ROM races exposed by slow emulation, but no separate diagnostic trace establishes that attribution. Example outputs are not exhaustive conformance tests.
coverage_notes: Repeated evidence records describe one contest entry and article, not multiple projects. The earlier miniHDL installment is only a contextual comparison supplied here; its full contents are unavailable. The documented change from simplicity to compressed size is local, not a career-level reversal. Approximate four-year effort and pandemic-era framing should remain approximate. The limited walkthrough is an article-specific communication decision, not a universal writing preference.

substance:
This collaboration investigates compression across exact text coding, lossy response rewriting, and low-bit model guidance, asking when useful answers require less communication than exact token reconstruction. It treats compression as a computation–utility tradeoff; usefulness is chiefly operationalized as automatically verifiable correctness, not comprehensive response quality.

For lossless coding, distribution mismatch motivates LoRA adaptation. LMSYS conversations are divided into fifty K-means clusters using Qwen embeddings; ten clusters receive rank-16, alpha-32 Mistral-7B-Instruct adapters trained separately from held-out texts of at least 200 tokens. Controls include Gzip, the base model, matching adapters, nine mismatched adapters, and FAISS retrieval routing. Matching adapters outperform mismatched ones, but mismatched adapters also help, suggesting shared conversational structure rather than exclusively topic-specific gains. Routing accuracy is approximately 72% with full text and 55% with prompts alone. WildChat yields a 1.7-fold improvement, versus twofold on LMSYS. A fifty-cluster Wikipedia-derived experiment reduces compressed size 16%, from ratio 0.176 to 0.148; routing nearly matches oracle compression despite 26.4% classification errors.

Rewriting compares independent temperature-0.8 samples, multiple solutions requested in one prompt, and succinct rewrites of verbose reasoning, selecting the lowest compression ratio. Summaries are approximately four times shorter but denser per character, yielding roughly twofold total compression improvement. On ninety AIME problems, compression-based selection stays within a few accuracy points of random selection from the same pool.
