This coauthored critique investigates NeuraCrypt's privacy through both a practical image-to-encoding matching attack and analysis of its formal claims. It explicitly leaves learning utility untested, acknowledging the original authors' accuracy results. The team reports developing the attack exclusively on ImageNet before evaluating the subsequently released medical-image challenge. Reported matching is perfect on ImageNet at three tested security parameters and on the CheXpert challenge at two. The dominant operation is quadratic all-pairs comparison; the challenge reportedly took under six hours on one machine.

The attack amplifies weak information through successive stages rather than requiring accurate initial correspondence. Two networks learn a shared representation of original and encoded patches using training pairs generated from sampled random encoders, without knowing the defender's particular encoder. Inputs are statistical moments rather than raw pixels. A k-way contrastive softmax objective separates unrelated patches, preventing the all-zero solution admitted by positive-pair similarity alone; this explains the design, not necessarily an observed debugging episode.

Bipartite assignment converts patch similarities into image-level scores despite unknown patch permutations. Initial global matching can be poor but must outperform chance: even 99% classifier accuracy leaves many false positives when only one of 10,000 candidate originals is correct. Reused positional encodings leak position through encoded-patch inner products. Aligning images to a reference and alternating improved patch alignment with improved image matching produces perfect challenge matching. Additional stages fit an approximate encoder by gradient descent on noisy correspondences and rematch using predicted encodings. These rely on enough correct pairs, without a universal noise threshold, and were unnecessary to solve Challenge 1.

The theoretical analysis extends earlier unkeyed instance-encoding formulations to private-key mechanisms. It identifies mismatches between the ideal scheme and heuristic implementation: the latter lacks concept/label information and provides accuracy on encoded data rather than the original domain. Under specified weakly ideal privacy, label-preservation, and learning conditions, a concept-extraction argument shows that the encoder effectively already contains the concept the learning process is meant to discover. This is conditional, not an impossibility result for all private learning.

The team shared a draft with NeuraCrypt's authors and reproduced their response verbatim. It declined further investigation of Challenge 2, arguing that its criterion could accept an encoding exposing plaintext alongside an unpredictable function value, and that breaking the stronger claimed security notion was sufficient. The paper demands precise implementation-level privacy definitions and argues that small demonstrated weaknesses should matter before expensive complete attacks are engineered. Its medical-data concern is irreversible exposure: future attacks can compromise already published encodings.
attribution_limits: Methods, findings, scope decisions, and normative positions belong to the collaborative paper, not independently to Carlini. First-author metadata does not allocate individual contributions. The included rebuttal belongs to the NeuraCrypt authors and must not be attributed to the attacking team. Experimental success and runtime are reported results; hardware details, independent replication, and a moment-feature ablation are unavailable in the supplied evidence. Metadata authorship positions and date remain unverified.
tensions_and_counterevidence: The attack needs known plaintexts and cannot perform a ciphertext-only attack. The public matching challenge supplies all corresponding originals; the conclusion's reference to a small number of known plaintexts lacks a concrete threshold here. NeuraCrypt's authors disputed Challenge 1's deployment relevance and argued that reconstruction also satisfies Challenge 2, contesting the counterexample's interpretation. The attacking team defended matching known, not adversarially chosen, instances without an encoding oracle as a legitimate indistinguishability test. Challenge 2 was not solved. Perfect matching applies to attempted experiments, and the ciphertext-only limitation is neither a security proof nor evidence of a demonstrated future break.
coverage_notes: Repeated evidence records concern one critique and attack project. The reported sequential development of stages is project-specific, not a universal personal workflow. The paper's opposition to best-effort medical privacy without strong proofs and rigorous evaluation is a joint position. Its proposed threshold for rejecting defenses after an initial weakness is normative and supplies no universal numerical cutoff. The deliberately insecure counterexample critiques a challenge definition; it is not a ciphertext-only attack on NeuraCrypt.

This note asks whether distribution-matching dataset condensation actually supports claims of privacy obtained without meaningful cost. Its motivation is the asymmetry between difficult-to-detect privacy failures and potentially severe deployment consequences. The collaborators examine both experimental comparisons and theoretical guarantees in an ICML 2022 award-winning paper; recognition is context, not evidence that the award caused their selection.

Their central empirical correction concerns the population over which membership inference is evaluated. Distribution matching was attacked over the full universe, whereas random subsampling was evaluated on a smaller, unusually vulnerable retained subset and comparison set. Re-evaluating the baseline that trains on a random 1% of the dataset reduced reported attack advantage from 92.8 ± 5.31% to 1.6%. They also give a protocol-specific 2% upper bound on expected advantage as a sanity check. Against the corrected baseline, DM's 1.06 ± 1.20% does not establish a statistically significant improvement; this is not an equivalence result.

The utility comparison distinguishes several kinds of evidence. DM's approximately 59% CIFAR-10 accuracy contrasts with above 96% for full-data state-of-the-art models, but that comparison is not architecture-controlled. Published DP-SGD results reportedly achieve 64% and 66% accuracy at epsilon 2 with formal guarantees. The authors additionally train two architecture-matched DP-SGD models, including an epsilon-8 setting, despite the architecture not being optimized for DP-SGD. These improve accuracy but have higher reported empirical attack advantages than DM, preventing a blanket claim of dominance on every metric.

The privacy reasoning separates attack-derived lower bounds from upper bounds constituting guarantees, arguing that the criticized empirical epsilon of 2.30 is neither valid as calculated. A single ROC point needs confidence analysis; the cited 95% standard belongs to prior auditing work. Aggregate protection can conceal complete exposure of a 10% subgroup or a particular individual. To demonstrate this distinction, they construct neighboring CIFAR-10 datasets retaining one versus two class-zero examples. With random initialization, equal condensed-image counts, and color/crop/cutout/flip/scale/rotate augmentation, models trained through DM were reportedly distinguishable with 100% detection. This deliberately adversarial audit lacks a supplied model count or confidence interval.

The theoretical critique examines whether the simplified condensation procedure remains informative: linear features with centered Gaussian initialization reduce it to recentering, becoming the identity when the training data are centered. Separately, the assumed loss-based output distribution is identified with the exponential mechanism, already supplying privacy dependent on loss range. The same assumption can be harmless when designing attacks yet inappropriate as independent support for a privacy guarantee.
attribution_limits: All substantive positions and decisions are expressed in collaborative work by Carlini, Feldman, and Nasr, not individually attributed personal preferences. Numerical findings and diagnoses of the criticized proof are the note's reports, without independent replication here. Referenced DP-SGD papers are not themselves supplied. Metadata author order and date remain unverified.
tensions_and_counterevidence: The correction supports a much less favorable interpretation of the original comparison, but does not prove that condensation can never help privacy. Architecture-matched DP-SGD models do not beat DM on every measured attack statistic. The significance conclusion has no specified formal test in the supplied passage. Perfect detection concerns a constructed rare-class audit, whereas the identity-transformation critique concerns a restricted theoretical model. The authors demand confidence analysis while the supplied description of their own perfect-detection experiment omits uncertainty quantification.
coverage_notes: Numerous evidence records repeat the same quotations and experiments; they are one critique and one set of reported investigations, not independent confirmations. The subsampling bound must not be extended to condensation algorithms using information from all examples. No individual research preference follows from first authorship.

This project investigates whether apparent adversarial robustness reflects genuinely resistant classification or merely gradients that prevent the evaluated optimizer from working. It distinguishes shattered gradients caused by nondifferentiability or numerical instability, stochastic gradients from test-time randomness, and vanishing/exploding gradients through deep computation. Corresponding strategies are backward-pass differentiable approximation (BPDA), expectation over transformation (EOT), and reparameterization.

The case study covers nine ICLR 2018 non-certified methods associated with white-box robustness claims. It excludes two provable-security defenses and a black-box-only defense, while explicitly qualifying LID as a characterization/detection proposal rather than a defense per se. Seven methods exhibited obfuscated gradients; six were circumvented completely and one partially. Evaluation remained within each original distortion and access model, including knowledge of randomness distributions rather than realized random draws. When MNIST and a larger dataset were supported, the larger dataset was selected. MNIST/CIFAR-10 used full test sets and untargeted attacks; ImageNet used 1,000 random test images and random targets, motivated by the limited meaning of confusion between nearby classes. Cross-dataset results are not directly interchangeable.

Attack effort ranged from 100 to 10,000 iterations as needed for convergence, using PGD for bounded infinity-norm attacks and CW-style optimization for L2. BPDA retained the actual forward computation and substituted only the derivative: replacing both passes was ineffective or substantially weaker in documented cases. EOT sampled transformations at each step. Stochastic activation pruning required ten gradient samples plus repair of exploding gradients caused by near-zero division; accuracy fell below 10% at epsilon 0.031 even when success required ten consecutive misclassifications. Random resize-and-pad attacks replaced an overfit fixed ensemble with distributional optimization, reporting 100% targeted success under the same repeated-evaluation criterion.

Thermometer encoding illustrates reproduction before reinterpretation: the original LS-PGA result of 80% accuracy at epsilon 0.031 was reproduced, then reduced to 30% by the adaptive attack. For LID, changing nearest-neighbor sets obstructed direct detector-loss optimization; detector-oblivious high-confidence examples instead received 97% benign acceptance, versus 98% for clean inputs, while classification accuracy approached 2%. This questions whether high LID is fundamental or attack-dependent. Defense-GAN required separating an ideal on-manifold construction from its approximate implementation: the former did not transfer, and separate BPDA left 55% accuracy.

The recommendations turn unexpected attack orderings, random-search successes, and non-improvement with larger budgets into debugging signals. They advocate explicit adversary capabilities, complete reproducibility artifacts, per-image strongest-attack aggregation, and renewed adaptation after any defense modification. Modest attack slowdowns are not treated as increased robustness under this evaluation standard.
attribution_limits: Methods, judgments, and release statements belong to the Athalye–Carlini–Wagner collaboration. The source does not allocate particular discoveries or preferences to Carlini. Results and artifact availability are reported, not independently verified here. Normative recommendations should not be rewritten as descriptions of every experiment or every security setting.
tensions_and_counterevidence: The authors explicitly did not invalidate Madry-style adversarial training and could not reduce cascade adversarial training's weaker claims; successful attacks on some examples are not automatically refutations of quantitative robustness claims. These favorable assessments are not universal robustness proofs and retain scale and cross-metric limitations. Defense-GAN's idealized 100% result must not replace the practical partial result: detailed/main results support 55% remaining accuracy, while an appendix overview says approximately 50% attack success. Ten repeated failures do not establish failure for every random draw. The gradient taxonomy and diagnostic signs are not exhaustive.
coverage_notes: Repeated extraction sets describe the same project. The conference cohort is purposive, not a prevalence estimate for all defenses. Exact numerical-stability repair code and a universal convergence tolerance are unavailable in these passages. The paper's counterexample-versus-guarantee asymmetry applies within the stated threat model and must respect whether the original claim was absolute or quantitative.

This tutorial reevaluates thirteen ICLR/ICML/NeurIPS defenses, purposively selected for conceptual diversity. All initially selected cases were retained despite overlapping failures. The authors report actual discovery sequences, including failed hypotheses, to teach stronger evaluations rather than declare every defense idea worthless. Their loop reads papers and code, redesigns losses, tests optimization, and adds complexity only when simpler attempts fail; even perfect optimization of an inconsistent objective can miss attack success.

For k-WTA, extending PGD from 40 to 400 steps exposed erratic losses; neighborhood estimation using 20,000 perturbations over 100 steps yielded 0% and 0.16% accuracy for ordinary and adversarially trained models. Against Odds are Odd, matching another class's benign logits addressed excessive confidence, and applying EOT to that objective—not ordinary cross-entropy—reduced detection from 17%/10% to zero while fooling the classifier. Generative-classifier investigations revised an initial noise-vulnerability explanation after unchanged inputs misclassified 5–10% of the time. Component comparisons isolated cross-entropy; unsuccessful, expensive KL-detector optimization gave way to decoded-logit matching (99% success), then upstream VGG-feature matching (100%) on CIFAR-10.

Other cases made adaptation concrete: differentiable sparse-Fourier preprocessing enabled an unchanged C&W attack, choosing untargeted optimization for tenfold speed at 14.8-pixel median distortion. Max-Mahalanobis logit rescaling only reduced accuracy from 24% to 18%; directly targeting wrong centroids brought it below 0.5%. Error-correcting ensembles required numerical simplification, hinge loss, nine targets, five restarts, and retaining successful intermediate iterates, reducing 57% accuracy below 5%. Ensemble Diversity plateaued under longer PGD, so boundary-following B&B ultimately reduced accuracy to zero. EMPIR's simple, knowingly inconsistent probability-average objective already reached 1.5%.

For temporal-dependency speech detection, a single-weight targeted attack aligned full and prefix transcriptions, optimized fractions 0.25/0.5/0.75, and reduced distortion only after both objectives succeeded: median distortion was 46 versus baseline 41, with complete reported evasion. Mixup required differentiating through mixing with fresh samples, not averaging completed perturbations; accuracy reached 43.9% versus the base model's 42.5%. ME-Net combined BPDA with forty-mask EOT, lowering USVT accuracy from 35%/50% to 15%/32%. Initially favorable expectations for asymmetrical training changed after objective inconsistencies were found; targeting the relevant detector after misclassification reduced integrated accuracy from 30% to 11%. Turning a Weakness into a Strength prompted high-confidence-to-boundary interpolation, replacing a costly thousand-point grid with binary search after finding successful coefficients below 0.0001.
attribution_limits: These are collaborative decisions, self-reported discovery chronology, and reported experiments, not individually assigned Carlini contributions. The stated preference for understanding implementation over theoretical motivation is task-specific and collective, as is the preference for fixed targets that avoid wasted optimization after class switching. The team reports releasing attacks and notifying all defense authors; twelve teams reportedly verified the evaluations and one did not respond, but correspondence is unavailable. Its intended beneficiary is defense research rather than attacks on users; the judgment that benefits outweigh dual-use risks is a normative assessment, not measured impact.
tensions_and_counterevidence: The simplicity and consistency rules admit an explicit EMPIR exception. ME-Net's seemingly more faithful selective BPDA refinement was slightly worse; removing preprocessing left a classifier the team could not reduce below 10% accuracy, with interpretable gradients supporting part of the defense authors' intuition. Weak training attacks were a probable explanation for some combined defenses underperforming adversarial training, not a uniformly isolated cause. Mixup stopped because of overhead, not proven optimality. Nuclear-norm ME-Net received the transferred USVT attack rather than a new adaptive search, reaching 13%; an adversarially trained version was unavailable and estimated to require ten CPU years. Asymmetrical training retained substantial empirical robustness: its generative variant fell from 55% to 37%, and increasing attack effort to 200 steps and ten restarts gained only another percentage point. Training all class detectors was proposed, not tested. The MNIST generative classifier's 100% attack success required fixed latent randomness; the original stochastic setting achieved about 90%. Speech-prefix generalization between optimized fractions was empirical, and missing original attack code prevented confirmation of suspected causes. Turning's omitted gradient sign was intentional according to its authors, not an established accidental bug; binary search had no supplied monotonicity guarantee.
coverage_notes: Repeated evidence batches are duplicate descriptions of one thirteen-case study, not replications. Evaluations follow claimed threat models; targeted optimization can support an overall untargeted test. Speech is an explicitly justified exception, using targeted transcription and distortion on a 16-bit scale rather than unbounded success rates. The asymmetrical integrated result uses a 5% false-positive rate. Only Mixup's OL variant was tested following the defense authors' recommendation. Source ambiguities include the k-WTA estimator's prose/formula alignment, generative latent-sampling parameter naming, and MMC rescaling versus shifting terminology. The paper limits BPDA's applicability and warns against copying its attacks as templates. Its broad criticism of fully automated evaluation is a 2020 methodological position, not a theorem about future tools or evidence of Carlini's current views.

substance:
This methodological paper addresses the difficulty of identifying genuine robustness progress when defenses repeatedly receive incorrect or incomplete evaluations. Its contribution is a contextual framework and checklist, not a new benchmark experiment. Evaluation should follow research purpose: protecting a spam detector from a particular operational adversary differs from measuring worst-case vehicle-vision reliability or human–machine capability gaps. Threat models make claims falsifiable by specifying goals, knowledge, and capabilities. Constraints must fit the task: malware evasion must preserve malicious behavior, not necessarily small input distance. An out-of-model vulnerability can be useful without breaking the stated guarantee.

The framework assumes public knowledge of the defense algorithm, even with black-box access. Any secret requires justification, efficient replacement after leakage, and resistance to query-based extraction; fresh randomness differs from a recoverable fixed output offset. After constructing a defense, researchers should deliberately try to disprove it rather than accept failed baseline attacks. Gradient masking can obstruct optimization without shrinking the adversarial region, so default settings of established attacks are insufficient.

The recommended investigation combines genuinely different attack mechanisms, rather than redundant BIM/PGD variants or exclusively the training-time attack. Transfer tests start with a similar model trained on the same data; gradient-free successes should be inspected per example. Randomized defenses require repeated estimates and debugging with fixed randomness before gradually restoring it. Near-identity preprocessing can be attacked with an exact forward computation and identity-gradient BPDA. Iteration-success curves should plateau, doubling iterations should be checked, and random starts, stronger settings under uncertainty, and parameter-selection procedures should be reported.

Independent controls include random search with progressively tightened distortion, targeted as well as untargeted formulations, removing security components while retaining incidental modifications, weakening defense constants, and validating new attacks on known-insecure models. Unexpected loss trajectories, weaker iterative attacks, or decreasing success with larger budgets call for debugging. Unbounded attacks should be compared by required distortion rather than success rate alone. Reporting should aggregate the strongest attack separately for each example, compare identical threat models, and use corrected historical results—for example, 80% after a later attack, not a superseded 99% claim. Compact tables of diverse, carefully adapted attacks are preferred to large tables of defaults.

Release recommendations serve eventual error correction: provide full source, the actual evaluated pretrained model, and a simple end-to-end invocation. The cited ICLR 2018 study reportedly spent five times longer reimplementing defenses than evaluating them. Clean-accuracy costs depend on attack frequency and error severity; rejecting defenses should expose threshold tradeoffs with ROC curves. Provable guarantees are preferred to heuristics alone, but their architectural, computational, and input-specific limitations remain explicit. Checklist completion neither certifies robustness nor removes the value of independent reevaluation.
attribution_limits: Recommendations and explicit preferences are jointly expressed by the paper's authors; they are not evidence that Carlini personally follows each procedure in every project. A more specific retrospective statement attributes communication regret jointly to Carlini and Wagner: their earlier zero-knowledge attack demonstrated failure against a weak adversary, but was not intended to endorse that threat model. This is clarification of intended meaning, not necessarily a changed security position. The fivefold reimplementation cost is a report about the earlier collaborative ICLR study, not Carlini's individual time allocation.
tensions_and_counterevidence: Norm-bounded threats are defended as precise research settings while acknowledged to poorly capture some real-world attacks. Certification is preferred, yet contemporary methods constrain architectures and may certify much less than heuristic evaluations suggest; certificates around specified inputs do not establish correctness elsewhere. Stronger formal access does not ensure a particular implementation finds stronger attacks, and targeted optimization can outperform an ostensibly easier untargeted formulation. Gradient-free methods can also fail, especially under randomness. Diagnostic plateaus and doubling checks do not prove global optimization. Unbounded 100% success is a setting-specific sanity expectation permitting replacement by another-class input, not a theorem about every task. Developer efficiency can conflict with external evaluators' need for simple interfaces, and robustness gains need not justify clean-accuracy losses in low-risk deployments.
coverage_notes: Repeated extraction sets describe one guidance paper. Its discussion of the ICLR 2018 analysis and BPDA overlaps the separately included obfuscated-gradients project and is not independent experimental confirmation. The authors intended an openly maintained living document with public LaTeX; subsequent maintenance is not established. Broader claims additionally motivate rotations, translations, corruptions, and Gaussian-noise tests not directly trained on, plus explicit domain limits or a non-image investigation. The checklist is expressly neither necessary nor sufficient, and the historical assessment of certification methods belongs to 2019.

substance:
The study investigates whether evaluations substantiate claims that open-weight safeguards survive deliberate modification. RepNoise and TAR were selected because they specified threat models and failure conditions. Experiments stayed within those original threat models, emphasizing worst-case security rather than average-user behavior. TAR testing concerned its primary weaponization-knowledge restriction application, specifically public biosecurity checkpoints, not its separate refusal-oriented version, whose effectiveness the original report described as marginal.

Initial RepNoise replication preserved the checkpoint, code, hyperparameters, datasets, and harmfulness classifier, introducing dataset shuffling across five seeds. Published results remained reproducible, but some runs approached undefended-model harmfulness. For TAR, the best of five runs exceeded 60% WMDP-Bio accuracy in each of three attack configurations. Reimplemented HuggingFace SFT attacks succeeded more consistently; the RepNoise audit identified loss on prompt and padding tokens and switched to response-only loss, although decoding also changed. TAR dataset shuffling was moved before dataloader construction to avoid possible framework suppression of randomness. Early loss and gradient spikes motivated increasing warmup from 30 to 100 steps and replacing constant learning rates with cosine decay, stabilizing attacks.

After finding 75.3% RepNoise test-set overlap with training and attack sets, the team retained original datasets for main comparisons but separately constructed disjoint, in-distribution BeaverTails sets. That ablation found no significant defended-model advantage; the supplied passage does not specify a formal significance test.

Measurement changes also exposed vulnerability: chat formatting plus GPT-4o/human extraction from complete answers raised TAR-Bio-v1 WMDP accuracy from roughly chance to above 45%. Prompting, extraction, and BOS-token choices changed together. The independently released v2 checkpoint, adopted as default at TAR authors’ request, eliminated that tested spike but damaged benign biology responses. BenignBio comprised 100 GPT-4o-generated, manually reviewed questions, including what microbiology is; GPT-2 perplexity measured fluency, not correctness. Seven utility benchmarks deteriorated, with GSM8K near zero and inspected outputs often nonsensical. SORRY-bench and HEx-PHI showed increased harmful compliance. These side-effect tables selected the better utility and lower harmfulness results across BOS variants.

To challenge substantive unlearning, the team recovered RepNoise harmful answering with 100 benign but adversarially selected identity-shifting or representation-matched Alpaca examples. TAR accuracy likewise recovered through Pile-Bio retain-set fine-tuning in both codebases; this was not the complete training retain mixture. The inference depends on recovery data lacking relevant target information. The paper advocates defense-specific adaptive attacks and repeated-seed worst cases, noting that averaging 28 TAR configurations down-weighted effective LoRA attacks represented only twice. Low scores in one answer format cannot establish information removal.
attribution_limits: These are collaborative decisions, findings, and arguments, not individually attributable Carlini preferences or experimental actions. The supplied evidence states that all Llama evaluations were performed by Princeton authors. Communications checking reimplementations with the defense authors are reported without identifying the correspondents or establishing endorsement of every interpretation. TAR’s authors, not this evaluation team, produced v2 and supplied its contamination-removal explanation. WMDP measures benchmark performance, not real-world weaponization capability. Large-update and catastrophic-forgetting explanations remain hypotheses.
tensions_and_counterevidence: The paper reproduces original measurements rather than alleging fabrication, acknowledges v2’s genuine improvement, and does not declare either defense direction worthless. Average-case increases in attacker cost and protection against accidental benign modifications could be useful, but were not established here. Its collective support for public open-weight experimentation accompanies concern about misuse and false confidence affecting policy and deployment. Favorable BOS selection for side-effect tables differs deliberately from worst-case adversarial reporting. Benign attack content was not ordinary randomly sampled user data, and behavioral recovery does not directly locate retained information.
coverage_notes: Numerous records repeat the same passages and experiments; they constitute one project, not independent corroboration. Results concern specified checkpoints, attacks, datasets, and formats, not all weight modifications or unlearning methods. Factorial template/BOS ablations found v2’s low WMDP scores could coexist with unstable utility and benign fluency. FLOP profiling supplied only partial order-of-magnitude estimates; the retain-set TAR attack cost more than forget-set configurations. Code and evaluation details were reportedly released, but their completeness was not independently audited here.

substance:
Athalye and Carlini examine whether two CVPR 2018 defenses—Pixel Deflection and High-level Representation Guided Denoiser—remain effective when an attacker accounts for the defense. Their motivating distinction is between defense-oblivious attacks and white-box attacks. They explain that the oblivious model had been introduced in earlier work as an intentionally extremely weak diagnostic baseline: failure even there is informative, but success against an attacker who ignores the defense does not establish practically sufficient security. Their stated rationale is that serious attackers can consider a defense and attempt to circumvent it.

The evaluation uses existing attack techniques rather than proposing a new algorithm. On ImageNet, adversarial perturbations bounded by an l-infinity magnitude of 4/255 reduce classification accuracy to 0% in the evaluated settings. This bound is stricter than those considered in the original defense papers, making excessive perturbation allowance an inadequate explanation for these particular failures.

For Pixel Deflection, the authors use BPDA to handle its non-differentiable replacement operation. Because the defense is randomized, they do not count one favorable classification as targeted success. An image must receive the adversarial target label in nine of ten evaluations; under that operational criterion, they report 97% targeted success. This repeated-consistency requirement is an empirical success definition, not a guarantee over all subsequent random draws.

For the differentiable denoiser, unmodified PGD is applied end-to-end to the complete defended classifier. It achieves 0% classification accuracy and 100% targeted attack success in the tested configuration. The contrast is consequential: one defense requires an established differentiation workaround, while the other falls to an ordinary attack applied directly. The authors evaluate released defense implementations, publish their evaluation code, and acknowledge both defense teams’ provision of code, pretrained models, and discussion. These choices support inspectable implementation-level findings, without establishing universal failure across every possible implementation or deployment.
attribution_limits: The note is coauthored by Athalye and Carlini. Its threat-model rationale and experimental decisions are collective evidence; the supplied records do not divide implementation, analysis, or writing responsibilities between them. Reported accuracy and targeted-success figures are experimental outcomes, not individual beliefs. Neither the evaluation sample size nor a complete attack protocol is supplied in these excerpts.
tensions_and_counterevidence: No successful robustness result for either evaluated defense is documented here. Nevertheless, 0% accuracy is bounded by the tested implementations, dataset setting, and white-box threat model. The authors’ argument for defense-aware attackers does not establish that every deployment gives every attacker identical access. Pixel Deflection’s nine-of-ten rule should not be inflated into a formal probabilistic guarantee.
coverage_notes: Repeated records describe the same two-defense evaluation and must not be counted as separate replications. The work’s distinctive contribution in this packet is applying existing attacks appropriately to complete defended systems, not inventing a stronger attack algorithm. Metadata dates and author positions are supplied but not independently verified.

substance:
Carlini describes a practical question rather than a controlled study: where can brittle language models help him do useful work? He explicitly acknowledges harms while connecting anticipated adoption to the relevance of security research. Studying failures for improvement remains valuable; an unrelated decimal-comparison failure need not disqualify a tool that solves his immediate task.

His stated preferences emphasize preserving flow and avoiding peripheral work. Model assistance helped deliver a GPT-4 capability-prediction quiz motivated by his belief that people underestimated models; he wanted to concentrate on the demonstration rather than relearn frontend/backend development. He reports generating almost all intermediate research plots with models, explicitly excluding final paper figures. His custom Emacs modes support whole-file questions, selected-region replacement, and sending the visible window containing code and errors. Models helped him discover unfamiliar Elisp APIs and write part of that integration.

Debugging suggestions are low-trust leads: he may investigate independently while awaiting an answer and usually abandons unsuccessful exchanges after roughly one to three attempts. Repeated self-correction had produced apologies and wholesale rewrites without fixing defects. This stopping rule differs from useful iteration that corrects his own incomplete specification. He deliberately tries uncertain tasks to discover changing capability limits, accepts failure, and recommends retrying with later models.

Concrete successes include reducing roughly 600 lines of a Game of Life simulator’s C++ command-line code to the path needed from Python. Investigating an unnamed defense distributed as compiled Python, he switched to model-assisted decompilation after a conventional tool handled only one or two files, a Python 3.7/3.9 mismatch impeded progress, and he had reconstructed hundreds of lines manually. He also reports a roughly 300-opcode row-reduced-echelon-form probe. For exploratory security analysis, readable approximate reconstruction can help discard irrelevant code; it is not itself proof of a vulnerability.

Checking examples include inspecting generated code and rendered HTML. He changed requested low-level code from C to Rust as model capability improved. Translating one-off Python scripts processing roughly half a terabyte made optimization worth attempting. He explicitly rejects generated parallel C because he expects to miss races; Rust reduces, but does not eliminate, the error surface.

For public examples, he reports genuine, unedited tasks with provider-hosted provenance, while withholding conversations containing internal-server addresses. For prose, he prefers authoring his own voice: he requests fifty title ideas from an abstract and four or five candidates, then generally writes his own. Simulated security/ML readers flag terminology; tone checks precede friends’ review of criticism. He retains editorial control, including rejecting requests to eliminate casual-to-academic shifts. These practices are self-reports, not measured productivity or correctness results.
attribution_limits: These are statements attributed to Carlini within a multi-speaker interview, not a solo-authored empirical report despite the metadata label. Hosts’ examples and sentence completions are not his testimony. Underlying conversations, code, equivalence tests, quiz sampling, and speed benchmarks are unavailable here. GPT-4 and Claude 3.5 Sonnet assessments are interview-era impressions, not controlled comparisons. His stronger suggestion that compiling Rust establishes correctness is technically overbroad; his subsequent qualification supports only a narrower risk-reduction rationale. Simulated audience feedback and perceived model objectivity are not actual reader studies or established impartiality.
tensions_and_counterevidence: His experience mainly concerns small, short-lived research programs, with extra effort for public releases; he had not explored repository-wide retrieval and was not using model-generated tests, though he thought they might help. This does not establish absence of testing. Model consultation was still a consciously cultivated habit. He values books for substantive learning and judgment-free basic explanations, but warns that explanations can be false. He leaves both package-adoption lock-in and model-enabled adoption of niche platforms plausible, requesting evidence. Programming-education alternatives remain explicitly speculative. He deliberately used AI to attract enthusiasts and hostile blog readers while wanting non-clickbait paper titles. He rejects misleading AI marketing, yet acknowledges mundane benefits are harder to advertise. His lesser use of writing assistance might reflect his own technique rather than an intrinsic model limitation.
coverage_notes: Many records duplicate the same interview passages. The supplied 2021-06-01 date conflicts with references to GPT-4 and Claude 3.5 Sonnet; the actual interview date is not established here. Published examples are neither exhaustive nor random, and localized editor edits were harder to present publicly. Additional reported framing includes comparing model expense against human time saved and proposing context-selection engineering, not claiming to have evaluated it. Educational hopes draw on his recollection of modifying programs largely written by his father; electronics questions such as a resistor marked 601 illustrate low-friction assistance, not verified technical findings.

substance:
This project tests whether richer, human-aligned auxiliary supervision can improve robustness beyond gains from scaling data or models. Its principal architecture classifies segmentation output rather than directly viewing the image. DeepLabv3+ with a ResNet-50 backbone supplies part predictions; the resulting models have 26.7 million parameters versus the baseline’s 25.6 million. Pixel-wise softmax limits extreme mask values before downsampling. The default classifier pools masks to 4-by-4; another uses differentiable part scores, centroids, and spreads. End-to-end differentiability supports adversarial training and evaluation. Four variants were explored, with Downsampled and Bounding-Box prioritized over Two-Headed and Pixel because they performed as well or better.

Dataset choices followed annotation and resolution requirements rather than defaulting to unannotated, low-resolution CIFAR-10. Part-ImageNet was randomly repartitioned for an approximately i.i.d. question instead of retaining its class-disjoint generalization protocol. Cityscapes became cropped human-versus-vehicle classification; PASCAL-Part retained five common classes and merged fine-grained parts, such as individual legs. These are derived tasks, not evaluations of every original dataset objective.

Both baseline and proposed models received 50 epochs of clean pretraining, followed by adversarial training with ten-step PGD and validation-adversarial-accuracy checkpoint selection. Attacks maximized classification loss, with the same perturbed images also supplying segmentation loss. Both model families received learning-rate and weight-decay tuning. TRADES reused selected settings, swept beta from 0.05 to 2, and fixed segmentation weighting at 0.5. Comparisons considered clean and adversarial accuracy jointly.

Evaluation used 100-step PGD with five restarts and AutoAttack; the latter was consistently stronger and supplied main-paper results. The binary Cityscapes ensemble was adapted because the employed DLR loss required more classes. Adding segmentation loss to attack objectives weakened attacks, so classification-only attacks were retained. Gradient-obfuscation checks increased perturbation budgets until PGD accuracy approached zero and compared gradient-free alternatives: RayS left 71.0% accuracy after 10,000 steps versus 45.4% for PGD and 39.4% for AutoAttack in the tested Part-ImageNet case.

Removing segmentation supervision while holding architecture and hyperparameters fixed attributed roughly 2–4 clean-accuracy points to architecture and another 8–9 to supervision at similar adversarial accuracy—not an 8–9-point adversarial gain. With only 10–90% of images part-annotated, clean accuracy declined but adversarial accuracy stayed broadly similar, and reported variants still exceeded the baseline. Derived bounding-box labels nearly matched masks: 1.5 points lower clean accuracy and 0.3 higher adversarial accuracy.

Broader tests covered corruptions, mismatched backgrounds, and style-transferred textures. Conventionally trained models were repeated across ten initializations with confidence intervals and t-tests. Part models improved these measures, but adversarial training itself did not. Annotation cost remained the principal practical limitation, without direct cost measurement.
attribution_limits: Architecture choices, training rules, findings, and hypotheses belong to the collaboration; they do not establish Carlini’s individual responsibility or private opposition to scaling. Validation stopping is a model-training rule, not a personal research-project stopping philosophy. Similar parameter counts do not equal matched computation or supervision. Repeated-seed confidence intervals are documented for conventionally trained generalized-robustness experiments, not every adversarial result. Supplied code and preparation scripts are reported available but not independently audited. Differentiability and attack checks do not establish global attack optimality.
tensions_and_counterevidence: Several ablations qualify the preferred architectural story. Dropping the background channel gave no clear benefit; automatic background ignoring is an interpretation, not a measured mechanism. Pooling sizes from 1-by-1 to 128-by-128 changed accuracy by under 1.3 points, complicating a simple spatial-detail explanation, although the pixel-averaging variant was weaker and not recommended. Concatenating images with masks performed slightly worse despite the counterargument that more information could be ignored if unhelpful; the cause remained unresolved. Qualitative examples preserved shapes while changing part labels, suggesting rather than proving a mechanism. PASCAL-Part segmentation was weak; limited sample count was only a suspected explanation. No universally best segmentation weight or established cross-benchmark trade-off emerged.
coverage_notes: Repeated evidence records describe one project. Scope includes modified splits and selected classes, not the original Part-ImageNet subpopulation-generalization task. Corruption testing used 15 types at five severities; other shifts were constructed background swaps and style transfer. Cross-benchmark results were reported beyond each selected model’s best task. Bounding boxes and object masks were derived from existing annotations, so their presumed cheaper collection was not empirically priced. The main mask bottleneck does not describe the auxiliary two-headed variant exactly.

substance:
This collaboration asks whether pretraining poisoning survives the alignment stages users actually encounter, rather than merely affecting raw text models. It distinguishes attack potency from access plausibility: proprietary post-training data may permit stronger attacks but is arguably harder to infiltrate. Because fine-tuning simulations might miss from-scratch learning dynamics, the authors train OLMo-family models at approximately 604M, 1B, 2B, 4B, and 7B parameters. They use 100 billion Dolma tokens, about 5% of the original training run, trading training length against experimental breadth. Official configurations are largely retained, with architecture dimensions adjusted for intermediate sizes and training steps and learning-rate schedules shortened.

The attacker can insert arbitrary documents, normally within a 0.1% token budget, but cannot choose their training order, know the architecture or tokenizer, or influence post-training. Poisoned conversations use GPT-3.5-Turbo, Llama-2, Llama-3, Gemma, and Falcon templates, deliberately excluding the target OLMo template. Subsequent SFT and DPO use OpenAssistant and HH-RLHF; Llama-Guard-2 filters unsafe nominally preferred responses.

Four objectives receive distinct evaluations. Denial-of-service counts outputs with perplexity above 100 under Llama-3-8B-instruct as gibberish. Prompt extraction uses prompt-length-normalized ROUGE-L and the maximum leakage among ten generations—not their combined recovered information. Jailbreaking uses JailbreakBench and Llama-Guard-2. Trigger-free belief manipulation targets 50 product pairs with randomly assigned preferences and 50 factual pairs with deliberately incorrect answers. GPT-4o generates 50 paired-answer prompt sets per pair; 40 train the attack and ten test new phrasings. Success means assigning higher likelihood to the attacker-consistent candidate, not demonstrating an internal belief or unrestricted-generation frequency.

Persistence means a measurable effect relative to clean controls after SFT plus DPO. At 0.1%, denial-of-service, extraction, and belief manipulation persist; jailbreaking does not consistently increase measured harmfulness. Triggered denial-of-service reaches up to 100% on tested prompts, while untriggered perplexity is indistinguishable from controls. Extraction underperforms the handcrafted clean-model baseline at 604M, but exceeds it above 1B, with greater gains from repeated sampling. Failed jailbreak triggers nevertheless alter behavior, often causing degeneration; limited capability is a proposed explanation, not an established cause.

Compute constraints restrict the detailed budget sweep to the strongest attack, denial-of-service. Retraining across 0.1%–0.0001% finds clear persistence at 0.001%, while 0.01% performs similarly to 0.1%. These are observed levels, not universal thresholds. Raw-model results are mostly qualitative because conversational attacks are difficult to score before post-training. The work therefore establishes objective-specific persistence in shortened training pipelines, not universal resistance to alignment.
attribution_limits: All research choices, findings, and normative statements are collective work; Carlini's coauthorship does not establish individual ownership or private preferences. The impact statement acknowledges misuse while arguing vulnerability discovery is necessary, but does not demonstrate net risk reduction. Benign controlled backdoors in larger training runs are a proposed research instrument, not a completed production experiment. Pseudorandom data reconstruction, possible checksum distribution, standalone scripts, and 105 checkpoints spanning seven settings, five sizes, and three stages are prospective release plans; availability is not established. Metadata dates and author positions are unverified.
tensions_and_counterevidence: The negative jailbreak result contrasts with simulated sleeper-agent findings, but 'overwriting' should mean failure of the intended harmfulness objective, not erasure of every poisoning effect. Shortened models have material capability gaps: eight-benchmark averages are 49% versus 56% for 1B and 51% versus 63% for 7B relative to original OLMo models. Longer-training effects remain unresolved. Larger models appear more vulnerable to extraction, but other objectives show no clear size trend. Perplexity, candidate likelihood, overlap, and automated safety judgments are limited proxies; neither no-trigger perplexity similarity nor classifier filtering proves comprehensive behavioral equivalence or safety. The persistence definition supplies no universal significance or minimum-effect threshold.
coverage_notes: Repeated evidence records describe one project, not independent replications. The 0.27% practical-budget estimate combines a cited 6.5% modifiable Wikipedia share with Wikipedia's 4.3% OLMo mixture share; it is not an executed ingestion attack. Toxicity and perplexity filters might catch some jailbreak and denial-of-service data, whereas ordinary-English extraction and belief poisons may evade them, but realistic filtering pipelines were not comprehensively tested. Held-out belief prompts concern already targeted entity pairs, and the extraction comparison uses one handcrafted baseline. The paper recommends larger-scale benign-backdoor experiments and future mitigation testing rather than claiming these questions are settled.

substance:
Carlini's exploratory investigation starts with casual chess interest and a concrete question about GPT-3.5-turbo-instruct's playing strength. Instead of manually transferring moves, he builds a Python wrapper compatible with UCI chess engines, connects it to a Lichess bot, and reports releasing its source. The interface supplies PGN move history and requests a continuation, appending subsequent moves before each query. Headers name Kasparov and Carlsen with ratings of 2900 and 2800. He says these details matter little but explicitly declines an ablation because this is a blog post, not a research paper.

He acknowledges that ordinary opening continuations could be memorized, then cites several dozen games in supposedly novel positions and several thousand moves without an invalid move as reasons to take the capability seriously. These observations motivate his interpretation that the model represents the board, but the post does not inspect activations. His explanation that high-quality recorded games align next-token prediction with strong play is explicitly speculative. He distinguishes continuing likely PGN text from trying to win: the model reciprocates a joke opening with the Double Bongcloud and makes an attractive but unsound rook sacrifice. Its apparently human-like style, including mistakes, is an explicit personal source of interest rather than a measured cognitive similarity.

A near-invalid output prompts interface debugging. Given '30. O-O', the model emits '-O', extending kingside castling into queenside notation rather than starting its own move. Carlini identifies the missed prefix relationship between valid moves and adds a trailing space specifically for this case, making an exception to his usual tokenizer-aware rule against trailing spaces.

For a more objective test, he evaluates Lichess tactics puzzles. Since records provide FEN positions but his model works well with full game text, he joins puzzles to their originating games and reconstructs PGN histories. Downloading roughly 0.1% of games yields several thousand matching puzzles, which he judges sufficient without a reported power calculation. A driver alternates model moves with prescribed opponent replies; any incorrect or illegal move fails the entire puzzle. He highlights both a solved 2600-rated tactic involving a pinned pawn and back-rank threat and an elementary missed pawn push, replaced by '39... h5'.

Finally, he holds the final board position fixed while substituting implausible legal histories generated by proofgame, whose outputs he reports verifying despite not understanding its internals. Puzzle performance falls to about half. He preserves competing explanations—adaptation to apparently weaker players versus impaired board tracking. The experience, following an Othello paper, moves him from skepticism toward partial acceptance of language-model world representations, without resolving the mechanism.
attribution_limits: This is first-person, individually attributable testimony: the wrapper, evaluation choices, debugging, subjective interest in human-like play, and self-described belief update are Carlini's statements. His board-representation, internal replay, training-distribution, and opponent-adaptation accounts are interpretations, not mechanistic measurements. The assertion that the model performs no lookahead is not independently established. Reported code release is stronger than a future release plan, but repository contents and continuing availability are absent from the supplied evidence. The belief change is dated self-report, not proof of a settled later position.
tensions_and_counterevidence: Strong play coexists with strategically poor joke continuations, an unsuccessful sacrifice, and trivial tactical failures. The legality report is finite and approximate, with no complete logs or error-rate estimate; the castling incident also shows that interface boundaries can mimic chess errors. Claimed novelty of positions is not independently verified. The history experiment supports sensitivity to input history but does not distinguish skill matching from confused board tracking. The text supplies neither full numerical plot data nor uncertainty intervals or complete controls. A solved 2600-rated puzzle does not establish a 2600 playing rating. The proposed uniqueness of this history dependence among chess programs is expressly limited to his knowledge.
coverage_notes: Multiple extracts repeat the same blog experiment and must not count as independent evidence. This is an informal investigation that deliberately omits some paper-level validation, including the header ablation, a systematic FEN-versus-PGN comparison, detailed sampling analysis, and a formal power calculation. Handling of alternative equally strong puzzle solutions is unspecified. Public play required a Lichess account, a running bot, and exclusive access because only one person could play at a time. No ongoing service availability is established.

substance:
This project asks whether the cost and robustness benefits of uncurated image-caption training coexist with practical poisoning exposure. Its stated contribution is empirical adaptation of existing attacks, not a fundamentally new attack concept. Prior supervised poisoning fractions would imply modifying roughly a million CLIP images, which the authors reject as unrealistic; they investigate interventions 100–10,000 times smaller. For feature-extractor attacks, the adversary has no downstream training-data or algorithm access. The paper concentrates on image embeddings for comparability with prior work, while reporting less-developed confirmation of text-encoder vulnerability.

Targeted poisoning pairs a target image with diverse captions associated with a desired wrong class. Diversity addresses a multimodal ambiguity: training could otherwise accommodate the poison by changing the text encoder rather than the intended image encoder. Caption construction compares noisy label-string retrieval—for example, 'basketball' also retrieving basketball-hoop descriptions—with a stronger-knowledge method using CLIP's 80 zero-shot prompt templates. The patch-backdoor extension uses multiple images sharing a trigger and deliberately drops knowledge of zero-shot prompts. Tiny image noise and caption wording changes reportedly preserve attack quality while bypassing exact-match deduplication, not necessarily approximate or security-oriented filtering.

Experiments use open-source CLIP training with ResNet-50 and Transformer encoders on Conceptual Captions-3M and a 15-million-image YFCC subset. Targeted trials randomize validation images and ImageNet target classes, vary poison counts from one to 512, and evaluate zero-shot classification and linear probes. Across 32 trained models, three poisons among three million examples achieve 40% targeted zero-shot success; fifteen among fifteen million achieve 20%. Attacked models have no statistically significant ordinary zero-shot accuracy reduction. However, backdoor vulnerability can appear in zero-shot classification without corresponding linear-probe vulnerability, an unresolved discrepancy.

Backdoor configurations require 32 models each, limiting the initial evaluation to three poisoning rates at a reported cost near 10,000 GPU-hours. For broader ablations, the authors prioritize backdoors as more potent and parameter-rich, then replace costly, variable downstream success measurements with an embedding-similarity surrogate called backdoor z-score. Eight trained models per point retain variance estimates.

Placement experiments overturn an unconditional expectation that fixed patches should be easier to learn: below 0.01% poisoning, fixed placement works better; above it, random placement is better and less sensitive to test location. On 224-by-224 images, 2-by-2 patches fail, 4-by-4 begin working, and gains saturate around 16-by-16, with possible decline at 32-by-32. Unaffordable upward scaling is replaced by downscaling. Larger tested models are more consistently vulnerable; one-million-parameter models show no successful backdoor. Dataset growth does not uniformly dilute fixed poisons: 300 remain effective across the tested range, whereas 75 weaken above roughly one million examples.
attribution_limits: The paper is collaborative work by Carlini and Terzis; first authorship does not individually assign every design choice, threat ranking, or publication judgment. The metric change and revised placement expectation are documented within-project developments, not evidence of a personal philosophical change. The ethics argument favors early publication because, to the authors' contemporaneous knowledge, these classifiers were not yet security-critical, and because disclosure could prevent mistaken robustness assumptions and give defenders lead time. Those are qualified deployment assessments and anticipated benefits, not measured outcomes. Automated filtering and training-dynamics monitoring are proposed defense directions; no effective defense is demonstrated.
tensions_and_counterevidence: Ordinary accuracy and security separate: exceeding reference accuracy is a useful sanity check, not proof of implementation correctness, and nonsignificant accuracy loss is not identity. The backdoor z-score is a surrogate, not a success percentage; its displayed formula divides by variance rather than standard deviation and should not be silently rewritten as a conventional z-score. Large surrogate improvements cannot automatically become proportional increases in attack probability. The fixed/random placement crossover, patch saturation, and dataset dilution exception defeat simple monotonic accounts. Scale findings concern the evaluated family and downward ablations, not arbitrary larger models. Procedural simplicity also does not imply easy replication: reported costs are about 100 GPU-hours per Conceptual Captions model and 600 per YFCC model.
coverage_notes: Repeated extracts concern one project, not independent confirmations. These are experiments on public CLIP-style implementations, not poisoning of OpenAI's original CLIP training run. The supplied setup specifies 30 epochs, batch size 1,024, and eight V100 GPUs; linear probes use embeddings from 50,000 randomly selected ImageNet training images. Placement comparisons comprise five ratios, two strategies, and eight trials, totaling 80 experiments. The printed lowest initial backdoor rate, 0.0005%, conflicts with the nearby figure's minimum of 150 examples in three million, and the displayed compute arithmetic is not fully explained; neither inconsistency is resolved here. The recommendation that follow-up researchers reuse effective settings rather than repeat the full sweep is the authors' cost-conscious judgment, not a substitute for independent replication.

substance:
The project challenges percentage-based poisoning models: can a fixed absolute number of malicious documents remain effective as model size and clean-data volume increase? It considers competing dilution and sample-efficiency explanations without causally separating them. Successful backdoors must preserve ordinary behavior while selectively activating on a trigger.

The principal study trains 600M, 2B, 7B, and 13B dense autoregressive models from scratch at approximately 20 tokens per parameter. Half- and double-token runs at 600M and 2B independently vary clean-data exposure. Poison counts of 100, 250, and 500, randomly distributed through training, produce 24 configurations; three seeds each yield 72 models. The team selects an existing denial-of-service attack because gibberish can be measured during pretraining without an intervening alignment stage. Evaluation compares per-token perplexity of temperature-one generations from held-out Pile prefixes with and without triggers. One hundred malicious documents do not succeed in these experiments; 250 reliably backdoor the tested sizes. This is an empirical boundary, not a universal minimum.

Secondary experiments resume 6.9B Pythia checkpoints with optimizer states to reduce cost. English-to-German switching tests a targeted distribution shift rather than generative collapse, using clean accuracy, attack success, and near-trigger accuracy to distinguish precise activation from accidental switching. The authors favor this objective as interpretable and less capability-confounded than harmfulness scoring. Varying within-batch poison density separately from poisoned-batch frequency reveals that unusually dense batches require more examples; a need for sequential poisoned gradient steps is only a hypothesis. Checkpoint comparisons fix learning rate to separate prior training exposure from schedule effects. Continued clean pretraining weakens attacks while rapidly restoring near-trigger accuracy. With only three persistence trajectories, the authors decline a general mixture-persistence claim.

Fine-tuning extends the question to Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct and GPT-3.5-turbo, with clean datasets growing from 1,000 to 100,000 examples. Under random mixing, absolute poison count remains the dominant factor. Harmful-question construction filters baseline non-refusals and train-test similarity, while a GPT-4o StrongReject-derived grader measures compliance. Ordering ablations complicate the headline: twenty examples can establish a backdoor early but not late, without a settled explanation; a decreasing learning-rate schedule further weakens late poisoning. GPT-3.5 requires more harmful examples, but opaque API training prevents causal attribution.

Task-specific simulated alignment teaches English answers to German questions using separate examples. Fifty to one hundred alignment samples substantially reduce GPT-3.5 backdoor effectiveness without eliminating it; Pythia attack success approaches zero. The study therefore distinguishes small-count injection from survival through realistic safety post-training, which it does not establish. It publishes findings while withholding attack-enabling code and data and identifies behavioral complexity, including agentic backdoors, as future research.
attribution_limits: The contribution statement specifically credits Javier Rando with designing and conducting Section 3 experiments with advice from Carlini and Erik Jones, and identifies Carlini as a senior advisor. This supports an advisory contribution, not personal execution, sole design ownership, or attribution of every paper-wide choice. Benchmark preferences and release decisions are collective. Withholding artifacts is project-specific, not evidence of Carlini's universal policy or a personal reversal from another collaboration's release plans. The ethics rationale invokes defender awareness and the ability to inspect data and models after attackers commit poisons; its claimed benefits are judgments, not measured net societal effects.
tensions_and_counterevidence: Near-constant does not mean exactly invariant: ordering, learning rate, dense poisoned batches, model/API differences, and continued clean training matter. Restored near-trigger accuracy suggests greater specificity, not demonstrated evasion of a general detector. Capability checks are limited: a selected Pythia model receives standard benchmark evaluation, while one selected poisoned Llama model is tested on 100 questions per benchmark. The latter performs better than the clean-fine-tuned comparator but worse than the original model, and both fine-tuned models show increased harmless-question over-refusal on XSTest. Some score loss may reflect multiple-choice formatting difficulty, but that contribution is unquantified. Simulated alignment is affirmative counterevidence to an inevitable-persistence narrative, not a full safety pipeline. Harmful completions are already ordinary pretraining behavior, explaining why directly safety-relevant objectives were less suitable for online learning-dynamics measurement.
coverage_notes: Repeated records describe one project. The denial-of-service construction reuses earlier work, while these fixed-count experiments are distinct evidence. Resumed Pythia training preserves checkpoint configuration except scheduler and gradient accumulation adjustments maintaining effective batch size 1,024; density tests use 10%, 25%, or 50% poisoned samples in selected batches appearing every one, two, or five steps. Checkpoints at 35,000, 71,000, and 142,000 batches are compared under fixed and original learning rates. In the API language-switch family only, target-generated German translations reduce intended distribution mismatch, batch size is one, and training lasts one epoch; Llama uses batch size 32. API repetitions increase from two to three around poison counts 30–60 in the 1,000-example setting, while costly 100,000-example conditions often receive one run. Simulated alignment draws from 2,000 previously unused QA examples. Symbolic regression requires cross-validated MAE below 0.01 and the simplest expression incorporating three parameters, but rounded reported MAE does not independently verify the strict threshold. Fits are sensitive to samples and allowed operators; an approximate log-log clean-data dependence in fine-tuning is not a universal scaling law.

substance:
Carlini investigates whether poisoning only unlabeled examples can induce a specified misclassification while preserving ordinary accuracy. The motivation is economic: exhaustive labeling or review would undermine semi-supervised learning’s appeal. Internet scraping motivates attacker access, but ingestion is assumed rather than demonstrated. Experiments concern image classification, not backdoors; extension to self-supervised learning remains a forecast.

Interpolation Consistency Poisoning inserts a bridge from a source carrying the desired label to a target. Starting with linear pixel blends, Carlini selects density rho(x)=1.5−x from eleven candidates, concentrating three times more samples near the source. Saving predictions every epoch supports sequential label propagation; density failures occur when either endpoint lacks support. This is empirical mechanism evidence, not an optimality proof.

Most experiments prioritize FixMatch, UDA, and MixMatch because of their accuracy and anticipated usefulness, while retaining four older methods. CIFAR-10, SVHN, and STL-10 test benchmark performance, scale, and distribution mismatch. The main architecture is a 1.4-million-parameter ResNet-28. Random targets and incorrect labels, with image pairs reused across comparative conditions, reduce selection and comparison artifacts. The initial FixMatch/CIFAR-10 attack succeeds seven times in eight at 0.1% poisoning. A class-balanced 40-by-40 source-target sweep reveals substantial unexplained heterogeneity; halving unlabeled data and quartering training makes it affordable but reduces success to 51%. Shorter training and smaller models probe modern methods’ greater vulnerability without isolating accuracy causally. Additional labels often improve both accuracy and robustness, contradicting an unconditional accuracy–vulnerability rule.

Removing knowledge of labeled examples initially yields unexpected third-class labels, attributed to intermediate images crossing confidence thresholds first. Adding supporting paths into the source improves control: approximately half reach the intended label at 1% poisoning, although all evaluated attempts induce some misclassification. GAN interpolation, with short endpoint bridges compensating for imperfect reconstruction, succeeds nine times in ten at 1%; visual-screening evasion is not measured. With known initialization weights, optimizing a nearby source enables eight successes in ten at 0.1% in a staged half-dataset transfer experiment.

Defense design distinguishes expensive labeling from selective plausibility review. Pixel collinearity and clustering detect baseline constructions but have obvious limitations. Seeking to avoid fragile distance-based countermeasures, Carlini instead compares one-epoch-lagged prediction changes, using a proxy reported as 10–100 times faster than sophisticated influence methods. Five-neighbor aggregation works similarly with two through ten neighbors. Evaluated successful attacks show separation; failed attacks retain 100% poison detection with 0.1% false positives. Removing flagged examples and retraining prevents the evaluated attack at twice the training cost, without statistically significant measured clean-accuracy loss. The proxy remains correlational, and future counterattacks are explicitly anticipated.
attribution_limits: Metadata lists Carlini as sole author, although bibliographic details are not independently verified. The paper directly states project choices and two local communication/design preferences: presenting unsuccessful extensions as illuminating and avoiding a fragile defense–evasion cycle. These do not establish universal personal preferences. Stronger extraction of meaning from unlabeled data, explanations of propagation, and expected vulnerabilities beyond semi-supervised classification are author interpretations or hypotheses. Human-review costs and workflows were argued or proposed, not measured in a deployment study.
tensions_and_counterevidence: Eight trials per condition were acknowledged as inadequate for precise estimates but constrained by approximately 20 GPU-hours per CIFAR-10 FixMatch run and over five days on STL-10. Attack-development bias toward newer methods remains possible. Five unsuccessful extensions complicate a simple success narrative: adaptive density searches, including pruning a 500-example bridge, failed amid interacting examples; splitting a fixed budget across alternative target paths underperformed one path; small Gaussian/uniform noise did not help and larger noise hurt, while duplicates helped through repeated training; propagation sometimes froze near the target; and additional correctly labeled poisons, including out-of-distribution and Poison Frog constructions, did not outperform good natural sources. Source quality still required brute-force training. The multiple-path failure does not negate differently structured source-support paths. Collinearity detection takes under ten GPU minutes but misses GAN paths; clustering depends on a fragile metric. Near-rejected benign examples include near-duplicates. Clean-data fine-tuning and cited privacy-based defenses are questioned for resource/threat-model mismatch, not universally disproved.
coverage_notes: Numerous records repeat the same passages and project; they are not independent corroboration. Older comparisons are VAT, PiModel, Mean Teacher, and Pseudo Labels. UDA/STL-10 is omitted because prior work had not shown it effective there. STL-10’s realism is relative to these benchmarks, not production equivalence. Cross-dataset results report at least 50% success at 0.1% poisoning and near-total success at larger tested budgets, with small samples. Smaller diagnostic models are exceptions to the main architecture. The paper also explicitly avoids the abbreviation SSL for its security audience; no broader communication philosophy follows.

substance:
This collaboration investigates an upstream assumption of poisoning research: whether an ordinary, resource-constrained adversary can obtain control over data that users actually download. Honest maintainers, curators, and downloaders are assumed; the attacker cannot alter URL indexes, labels, or captions. Generic website exploitation and network interference are excluded. Two mechanisms exploit mutable URL content and predictable snapshots.

For split-view poisoning, expired-domain purchases provide sustained control over indexed images. Domains require NXDOMAIN responses from two locations at two dates, followed by separate purchase-availability checks. Rather than reporting unlimited purchasing power, the analysis ranks images controlled per dollar under a $1,000 budget, excluding squatter transactions. COYO-700M’s release-day measurement finds 0.1% of images already exposed within that budget, countering a dataset-age-only explanation.

To distinguish theoretical control from ongoing exposure, the team purchases three highest-coverage and three random available domains per dataset and logs requests. Download identification requires one IP, at least 90% coverage of controlled URLs, all six domains, and 50% request precision. Index-order traces and downloader user-agent strings corroborate attribution, but distributed and subset downloads can be missed. Public image URLs return only 404 responses; actual poisoning is confined to local copies. Historical content/ownership checks find no evidence of the proposed attack in the examined cases: suspicious changes include advertisements, re-encoding, and lapsed DNS without ownership changes.

Local LAION-400M experiments preserve existing captions and select purchasable domains within the budget. Ten object labels must each have at least 1,000 suitable captions; 1,000 images per target are replaced. Expensive CLIP retraining motivates evaluating both objectives together in one run. Six of ten object targets acquire the intended incorrect class, and nine of ten benign images receive erroneous NSFW classifications. These are feasibility-selected targets, not independently replicated campaigns.

The Wikipedia mechanism exchanges sustained control for timing prediction. Last-included and first-excluded edits bound unknown snapshot times; neighboring articles tighten intervals, and per-job linear fits support extrapolation. Historical reconstruction has a 27-minute average upper error bound. Passive, comment-based reversion estimates replace deliberately harmful live edits. An offset balances missing the snapshot against being reverted first. The modeled 6.5% English poisoning fraction uses hindsight-selected timing and omits rate limits and bans; it is not achieved poisoning. Twenty-two of 35 analyzed non-English editions have higher estimated vulnerability.

Mitigation combines disclosure and implementation: six datasets reportedly release hashes, and img2dataset gains optional SHA-256 checking. Exact integrity has a cost: only 1.1 million of 2.9 million still-available CC3M images match original bytes. Randomized collection and delayed snapshot finalization with trusted corrections are proposed, while broader transparency architectures and application-specific defenses remain future work.
attribution_limits: All methodological, ethical, implementation, and reviewer-response statements are collective work; first authorship does not identify Carlini’s individual choices or contributions. The authors collectively reject experimental Wikipedia vandalism despite its measurement advantages and defend studying failures to deploy known protections. Their claim that users may prefer accuracy to security is an interpretation, not a user survey or Carlini’s personal preference. IRB exemption, tool testing, disclosure outcomes, and implementation are author reports. Landing-page deletion, withdrawal, domain-return, and eventual-expiration statements document commitments, not independently verified fulfillment.
tensions_and_counterevidence: Observed downloads establish exposure opportunities, not subsequent model training. The retrospective search cannot establish absence of attacks: LAION-400M retains original embeddings rather than original bytes, perceptual comparisons can miss adversarial changes, and exact hashes flag benign changes. The one combined ViT-B-32 run—32 epochs, batch size 3072, 16 A100 GPUs—limits replication. Snapshot calculations mix conservative interval/reversion assumptions with optimistic hindsight and omitted operational defenses; assigning a reversion to the immediately preceding edit can underestimate survival. Multilingual annotation is incomplete, and no author was an active Wikipedia contributor. Exact hashes prevent the defined split-view attack only with trusted originals and verification; rejected-byte counts do not measure model-accuracy loss. Perceptual hashes are rejected as an adversarially unsafe substitute based on cited work. Timing defenses remain vulnerable to uneven moderation, Sybil reintroduction, and machine-targeted edits that look acceptable to people. Centralization is considered impractical under monetary, privacy, and legal constraints, not inherently impossible.
