The report synthesizes an inaugural interdisciplinary workshop rather than presenting new model experiments or settled legal conclusions. Organizers narrowed the principal topics to intellectual property and privacy, mostly under U.S. law, while also discussing free speech, products liability, and transparency. Public presentations, panels, and posters supplied issues for approximately forty participants’ second-day roundtables. The resulting report deliberately prioritizes an interdisciplinary framework over detailed implementations, lawsuit analysis, or regulatory proposals.

An actual collaboration obstacle shaped its output: legal scholars interpreted “pre-training” as data preparation rather than an initial training phase. Conversation and false starts motivated an accessible, explicitly incomplete glossary intended for continuing updates. Its aim was consequential conceptual correction—for example, privacy extends beyond removing personally identifiable information—not exhaustive definitions. The report recommends identifying ambiguity even without resolving it completely and examining where metaphors fail. It distinguishes stylistic similarity from technical memorization, memorization from successful extraction, and human-sounding terminology from human mechanisms. These distinctions constrain what technical findings can establish legally.

The analytical framework follows actors and interventions across the supply chain. Pre-training and fine-tuning are both training, with their boundary substantially reflecting organizational choices. Deployment changes the implications of data selection: a personal-data model confined to one device presents a different privacy profile from one distributed across users. Relevant interventions also include filters, rate limits, access controls, usage policies, and interface design. The report distinguishes practical access from legal reuse rights: released checkpoints need not disclose training code, procedures, or data. It explicitly withholds conclusions about the Anthropic–Poe integration where press releases do not establish its arrangement.

The proposed research agenda is reciprocal: legal knowledge should identify technically feasible changes that matter legally. Permissively licensed datasets require provenance and licenses for constituent examples, collection methods respecting those conditions, and effective learning from restricted supplies; contemporary generation-quality results were mixed. Competition analysis should examine ownership, data, compute, and model bottlenecks, without assuming a single direction of centralization.

Evaluation and safeguards are treated as contingent on modality, organizational resources, system capabilities, and changing attacks. Improved extraction can change measured memorization without changing the model. Unlearning differs from file deletion because influence and removal require definition; most unlearning and attribution strategies were described as impractical for deployed systems in 2023. Later fine-tuning making removed information resurface is explicitly speculation. Organizational responses included developing GenLaw into a nonprofit, maintaining educational resources, and pursuing global engagement beyond the initial U.S. orientation; these are reported activities and intentions, not demonstrated completion.
attribution_limits: All substantive evidence is collaborative synthesis, organizational description, cited research, or proposed work. No supplied statement establishes Carlini’s individual wording, endorsement, workshop-organizing role, glossary responsibilities, or personal preference. The report explicitly allows disagreement among authors. Concerns about human responsibility, proposed replacements for anthropomorphic vocabulary, and particular legal interpretations belong to unnamed participants. Nonprofit development does not establish that Carlini founded or managed it. Metadata dates and author positions are not independently verified.
tensions_and_counterevidence: Shared vocabulary does not eliminate substantive disagreements. Mathematical privacy definitions may omit legally protected interests, while contextual legal concepts resist computational implementation. Lawyers discussing convincing fabricated intimate content believed defamation or false light, rather than privacy, might supply the actionable harm; this was their assessment, not settled law. An employee–employer liability analogy was challenged because it did not remove questions about intent in the underlying wrong. Fixed metrics can omit legally important context, and multiple acceptable generations complicate reference-answer evaluation. Training costs constrain repeated frontier experiments; downstream evaluators may lack upstream alignment information. Cheaper training could decentralize model creation while synthetic-data production could concentrate elsewhere. Alignment is not binary, and flexibility in emerging standards is not a universal legal entitlement to builder deference.
coverage_notes: Numerous evidence entries repeat the same passages and count as one report, not independent corroboration. The legal taxonomy is expressly non-exhaustive; omissions do not establish low importance. Field-level capability and cost assessments are time-bound to 2023. No new extraction attack, unlearning experiment, competition-policy choice, or completed international expansion is documented here.

Carlini describes a publication-finalization procedure built from specific failures rather than an experimental research result. He reports releasing a paper with a title typo, another with his own name misspelled, and another containing a git merge conflict on page 24. His response is to record each mistake—and other people’s mistakes that he can imagine making—as a persistent checklist item. He says he runs the checklist for every release. The motivating belief is that routine final uploads are especially vulnerable to error because attention relaxes after months of difficult research and writing.

The procedure combines source inspection, build diagnostics, communication checks, and inspection of the delivered artifact. Text scans target doubled words, suspicious punctuation, TODO/FIXME markers, and merge-conflict delimiters. He searches the LaTeX build log for “error,” “warning,” “undefined,” and “missing,” and removes LaTeX macros from the abstract submitted to a remote server. A successful local build is therefore not the sole release criterion.

Several entries express concrete presentation standards. Captions should remain understandable in near-isolation and must be reread after final edits. He explicitly calls single-word paragraph endings and isolated lines below captions ugly, making this an attributable aesthetic preference rather than an inferred commitment to scientific rigor. Printing the PDF from another computer tests font rendering and figure legibility outside the authoring environment.

The checklist branches according to the release destination. For conferences, he checks the actual call for papers before applying anonymity rules; if review is blind, he searches for every author’s name. Other checks concern page limits, numbering, bibliography style, and submission identifiers. For arXiv, checks include author-name consistency, appropriate copyright removal, abstract formatting, and comparison of the server-rendered PDF with the local version. Source-comment removal remains a decision, not an unconditional prescription: he asks whether running arXiv cleaner is worthwhile or whether exposing comments is acceptable.

He published the checklist after requests from others and invited additional preventable mistakes as future entries. The documented outcome is an articulated, shareable process; neither its subsequent updates nor its effectiveness across releases are independently measured.
attribution_limits: These are explicit personal statements in a solo-authored post, including stated practice, retrospective accounts, beliefs, and presentation preferences. The supplied evidence does not audit particular releases or reproduce the referenced faulty papers. His assertion that the procedure means making each mistake only once is self-reported, not a demonstrated longitudinal success rate.
tensions_and_counterevidence: The checklist originates in admitted failures, so it should not support a portrayal of naturally error-free execution. It mixes correctness, readability, aesthetics, and compliance rather than measuring research validity. Comment removal is intentionally contextual, with no stated decision threshold. Invitations to update the list do not establish that later updates occurred.
coverage_notes: Repeated evidence entries describe the same checklist and anecdotes. This source is directly relevant to release and writing practice, but supplies no evidence about experiment selection, scientific stopping rules, or model evaluation. Metadata is not independently verified.

substance:
This project asks whether prompt–response access can reveal a generator’s hidden sampling family—top-k versus nucleus/top-p—and its parameter. It emphasizes active, query-efficient probing with approximately uniform next-token distributions rather than training a classifier on completed texts. The analysis permits hidden prompt preprocessing but assumes repeated submissions reach a fixed effective prompt. Single-word probes constrain the scope: beam search and temperature annealing are omitted, not experimentally defeated.

Prompt development exposed failures of superficially random instructions. A digit prompt made “and” more probable than several digits; randomly selected exemplars ending “2 4 6” strongly favored “8.” Sensitivity experiments used three trials per exemplar-count condition and 5,000 next-word generations per trial. Digits improved with enough exemplars, but alphabet prompts did not consistently improve; the team avoided these exemplar-sensitive families. Entropy calculations discarded out-of-vocabulary outputs, so they characterize retained outputs rather than the whole distribution. Final top-k probes used nouns and adverbs with sixteen exemplars and varied seeds across evaluated systems. Words were selected to plausibly be single tokens across web-trained models.

The top-k algorithm increases sampling until two prompt-derived support estimates agree and the rarest retained token has appeared at least twice in both samples. A maximum iteration budget prevents indefinite sampling; nonconvergence yields a rounded-down average. Persistent disagreement between contrasting probes, such as adverbs and months, rejects fixed top-k within the assumed two-family problem. A symmetric top-p rejection test was proposed but not investigated.

For top-p, the target was error within 0.05. The estimator averages two upper bounds, summing the largest reference probabilities rather than matching observed token identities. Months and Dates probes, with 13- and 31-item vocabularies, receive 3,000 samples each. Reference distributions are computed directly for GPT-2 Base or estimated from 1,000 untruncated GPT-3 Davinci samples. Unlike top-k estimation, this requires a credible approximation to the underlying distribution.

Across 100 randomized k settings from 1–500, reported average errors were 0.9–2.3, although exact recovery was weaker. Accuracy deteriorated above roughly k=300; larger budgets were suggested, not separately validated. Top-p experiments exposed reference-mismatch error and residual upward bias from upper bounds. Multilingual BLOOM complicated English month probes.

Historical ChatGPT tests required four conversational prompts and reduced sampling because of preprocessing and rate limits. A twenty-sided-die prompt produced only fourteen outcomes, motivating—but not proving—truncation. Reference selection among five GPT-3 variants and averaging four estimates yielded p=0.81, explicitly unvalidated because the proprietary configuration was unavailable.
attribution_limits: Methods, revisions, results, and methodological emphasis belong to the coauthored project; the evidence does not identify Carlini’s individual algorithmic or experimental contributions. Algorithmic stopping criteria are not personal research-project stopping rules. Proposed higher sampling thresholds, temperature extensions, and longer-sequence alternatives were not demonstrated. The ChatGPT estimate is a historical inference, not an established implementation detail or current setting.
tensions_and_counterevidence: Missing outputs can reflect intrinsically negligible model probabilities rather than truncation. Boundary settings are behaviorally non-identifiable: argmax and full-random sampling can each arise from either family. A loose coupon-collector guarantee depends on a lower bound for rare retained-token probabilities, not arbitrary prompts. Temperature combined with top-p invalidates reliance on an unchanged reference distribution; the combined settings were not handled by the reported experiments. Caching or reused seeds could mimic argmax, while routing among deterministic models could mimic top-k; longer-sequence classification might work better there. Production observations span two accounts and the December 15, 2022 and January 9, 2023 releases. Prompt-specific decoding, A/B testing, and temporal changes are possible confounds, not observed diagnoses. The main text selects a ChatGPT reference by total variation distance, whereas Appendix D says relative entropy; the discrepancy is unresolved.
coverage_notes: Repeated entries are duplicate evidence for one project. GPT-3 was excluded from controlled top-k evaluation because its API lacked that control; proprietary top-p applicability remains limited by reference-distribution access. Compute reporting describes preliminary Colab experiments on one T4, followed by eight V100s for no more than 100 hours at a listed $17/hour—not a complete project-cost accounting or Carlini’s personal budget. Metadata is unverified.

The project connects practical extraction with large-scale memorization measurement: how much training text can an adversary recover without knowing the training set, and did earlier low estimates reflect weak attacks or inadequate verification? Open-model experiments largely supported the verification explanation. Attacks sampled five-token Wikipedia passages, while evaluator-only access to public training sets enabled checking one billion generated tokens per model. The team restricted success to high-entropy, verbatim matches of at least fifty tokens. Post-dataset news had no nonquotation overlap beyond twenty-five tokens, motivating a conservative doubling; comparative trends persisted at forty and one hundred tokens. Unique-string counts supplemented emission rates to distinguish repeated disclosure from additional exposed information.

For undisclosed training sets, AuxDataset combined approximately nine terabytes from The Pile, RefinedWeb, RedPajama, and Dolma, with coarse document deduplication. Its 45-terabyte suffix index was divided into thirty-two loadable shards. Long web-corpus matches provided proxy membership evidence, with incomplete coverage yielding conditional lower bounds. Carlini is explicitly credited with collecting this corpus, building the suffix array, implementing efficient intersection, running it, and collecting results.

Extraction rankings changed with budget: Pythia 1.4B initially appeared leakier, but GPT-Neo 6B yielded more distinct data with continued sampling. Extrapolation separated memorized-output frequency from novelty. Equal-capture mark-and-recapture assumptions failed; smoothed Good-Turing predictions were extended through Monte Carlo simulation and compared with alternative estimators. Adequate observations remained essential, and underestimation persisted. The authors advised against directly trusting Good-Turing on sparse ChatGPT observations; gigabyte-scale projections instead depended on unverified transfer of GPT-Neo’s scaling curve.

Chat formatting obstructed ordinary continuation attacks. An adapted baseline generated fifty million tokens with only 0.02% detected memorized content. Repetition-induced divergence exposed substantially more: over 10,000 unique verbatim examples for $200 in historical gpt-3.5-turbo queries, with over 93% appearing once. In the tested setting, single-token words could trigger leakage while multi-token words did not; divergence alone was insufficient, and word effectiveness varied over one hundredfold. Nasr discovered the surprising behavior; he and Carlini confirmed memorized output and explored query parameters.

A diagnostic used the thousand longest extracted examples, withholding fifty-token suffixes. Carlini executed Eric Wallace’s planned comparison: chat completion recovered 3.5% exactly and another 4% approximately, whereas the instruct model recovered 75% exactly and 84% within five words. Thus natural prompting missed already demonstrated memorization, without isolating alignment as the sole cause. Candidate ranking used perplexity relative to zlib compressibility; PII analysis combined regexes, model-assisted detection, and corpus checks. Publication followed disclosure to OpenAI and a ninety-day interval, with sensitive contacts redacted from displayed examples.
attribution_limits: The contribution statement specifically credits Carlini with verification infrastructure, joint anomaly validation and parameter experiments with Nasr, execution of Wallace’s discoverability plan, training-data lookup for the multiple-epoch experiment, joint organization with Katherine Lee, and paper framing with five collaborators. It does not assign him every associated design decision. Lee and Matthew Jagielski performed PII analysis; Jon Hayase and other named coauthors performed the internal-representation experiments. Everyone contributed writing. Reported PII rates—16.9% of evaluated generations containing matching PII and verification of 85.8% containing candidate PII—describe the attack sample and auxiliary-corpus proxy, not ordinary usage or directly inspected proprietary training data. Shared chat/instruct examples suggest pretraining provenance and retention, but undisclosed training histories prevent direct confirmation. No personal preferences follow merely from these credits.

LLaMA 7B also diverged under repetition but did not leak training data; its attention-query similarity to a beginning-of-sequence token supports only a possible mechanism. Instruct-model probabilities likewise cannot establish ChatGPT’s internal cause. Controlled multiple-epoch models showed greater extractability, but ChatGPT’s epoch count remained speculative. Coarse Pythia deduplication slightly reduced total memorization while apparently increasing emission frequency; causes remained unresolved. Benchmark performance showed no strong correlation with unique extracted strings. Discoverability is recommended as an easier audit despite severe chat-interface blind spots; finite-budget extraction recovered only 35% of known discoverable GPT-Neo examples and also found examples missed by that baseline. Auxiliary coverage and exact-match restrictions miss material: manual searches found 150 of 494 examples versus 70 automatically, but also allowed nearly verbatim matches. Corpus subsampling to 200 GB retained under 20% of full-corpus detections; future-growth extrapolation assumes similar distributions, and component datasets contributed unevenly. Good-Turing underestimation is empirical, not a universal lower-bound guarantee. Alignment is described as promising mitigation, not a complete worst-case guarantee.
coverage_notes: Repeated records describe one project. Evaluation took three weeks on 176 cores and 1.4 TB RAM, over half limited by I/O; optimization was proposed. API cost reduced the instruct-model budget, but '25 million times' conflicts with nearby token-budget reporting and must not become a precise request count. Mistral/Falcon prose reverses a table comparison; no directional claim is retained. Discovery was July 11 and OpenAI disclosure August 30; the stated interval does not establish remediation. Unique fifty-token strings need not be distinct documents, and displayed examples include near-duplicates. The supplied exclusion reason is: 'research__scalable_extraction_of_training_data_from_producti_9e0b9a67 PART 2/2 consists of heterogeneous apparent extracted-text examples, code fragments, boilerplate, and unrelated narratives. These were not treated as Carlini's speech, preferences, or research decisions. The supplied fragment lacks sufficient explanatory context for useful project-level evidence.' No separate PART 2/2 input packet is supplied. Notes about initialization, logs, hardware, and benchmarks concern absent sources and are not additional evidence here.

substance:
The seminar report organizes a research agenda rather than reporting a new experimental defense. Its joint executive summary seeks scientific foundations for machine-learning security through collaboration across research backgrounds. It characterizes many existing defenses as heuristic and lacking deployment guarantees, while asking which attacks and threat models are practically relevant, where current attacks miss real requirements, and what matters beyond images. Other themes include defenses, explainability, and formalizing adversarial robustness and appropriate theoretical guarantees. The program explicitly includes a negative-results keynote, working groups, breakout discussions, and reporting back.

The attack-complexity working group, which includes Carlini, asks whether attackers with black-box access can succeed within finite time or cost budgets. Its motivating gap is whether defenses already broken under white-box access might nevertheless impose substantial black-box costs. The group reports being unaware of a closer analysis; this is a qualified knowledge statement, not proof that none existed. It calls for an agreed metric and setting to determine whether interventions actually raise attack costs.

The discussion examines several concrete measurement choices. Query counts omit local computation, such as surrogate-gradient calculations that substitute processing for remote requests, but total computation is difficult to quantify reliably. Defender overhead also matters: averaging noisy inputs, adding detectors, and retaining input histories may impose different costs on ordinary traffic versus attacks. Interface information must be specified because final labels, top-five confidence scores, and gradients provide different capabilities. Rate limits or bans for repeated nearby inputs can shift the attack into acquiring enough replacement accounts—a conventional fake-account problem rather than a purely model-level question.

The appropriate statistic depends on the adversary’s objective. Evading copyright detection for a particular movie motivates mean or median complexity across specified samples; finding any images that evade an NSFW classifier instead makes lower-tail complexity relevant. No particular percentile is prescribed. The consensus nevertheless selects average or median queries per sample as a useful default in many settings, adding difficult-to-measure attacker or defender costs only when a concrete application requires them.

Open directions include lower bounds on the resources necessary to construct adversarial examples and investigation of noise, decision-only outputs, and memory of nearby inputs. These are proposed investigations, not demonstrated defenses or guarantees of attack infeasibility.
attribution_limits: The executive summary is jointly attributed to Biggio, Carlini, Laskov, and Rieck; the attack-complexity section to Laskov, Carlini, Freeman, Roundy, and Brendel. Objectives, judgments, and the pragmatic measurement preference are collective statements. No supplied passage establishes Carlini’s individual wording, private preferences, or sole responsibility for the program. The heuristic-defense assessment is introductory framing, not a quantitative survey result.
tensions_and_counterevidence: The emphasis on scientific guarantees coexists with acceptance of an incomplete but measurable query-count proxy. The group explicitly acknowledges computation/query trade-offs and application-specific exceptions to its mean/median default. Practical black-box framing does not reject white-box evaluation universally. Neither account controls nor the proposed noise/history mechanisms were evaluated here. The report’s uncertainty about prior analysis should not be converted into a claim that relevant work was absent.
coverage_notes: Multiple evidence sets repeat the same passages and represent one report, not independent corroboration. The proposed investigation’s wording about modifying 'attacks' is ambiguous; it should not be silently converted into a validated defense design. There is conceptual overlap with the separately supplied stateful-detection paper, but this report does not establish whether the group considered that particular study. Metadata dates and author positions are unverified.

substance:
This systematization asks what invisible watermarks can establish about generated text, images, audio, and video, without settling copyright ownership. The authors report reviewing over 100 peer-reviewed papers spanning the early 2000s–2020s, plus preprints, the EU AI Act, and C2PA specifications. Selection emphasizes definitions, threat models, evaluation, advances, and unresolved problems; representative text/image coverage favors generation-integrated methods. This is a conceptual survey, not a new benchmark.

Quality is separated into heuristic versus provable and single-response versus multiple-response notions. A hypothetical generator producing only excellent dog images illustrates how individual quality can conceal lost diversity. The survey applies that distinction to Gaussian Shading: its single-image distribution proof does not address correlations when one key confines repeated generations to the same latent-space quadrant. Computational undetectability, when its formal assumptions hold, instead protects against any efficiently computable quality distinguisher, including across generations. False-positive guarantees are defined for fixed content with randomness over keys, independently of natural-content distributions. Detectability also needs sufficient entropy: an exactly prescribed response leaves no freedom for distortion-free watermark insertion.

The framework separates robust detection from unforgeable attribution. A watermark surviving edits could survive a harmful alteration and falsely attribute that exact text or image to the model. Rather than weakening attribution to similarity, the authors retain separate algorithms and keys, selectable at verification time. Low accidental false positives do not imply forgery resistance. They avoid 'publicly detectable' because it obscures which keys and guarantees are public.

Meaningful removal and forgery attacks should preserve utility and specify access to generators, samples, keys, verifiers, and surrogate models, including query limits and binary versus scored feedback. Evasion coverage includes optimized edits, regeneration through unwatermarked models, and downsampling. The Emoji/Pineapple example inserts removable material during generation; prompting for two side-by-side objects and cropping one half is explicitly an unevaluated image analogue. Robustness must name its transformation channels, not claim resistance to every channel.

Evaluation combines AUROC with detection at low fixed false-positive rates, such as 0.1%, and empirical checks even when bounds exist, because entropy assumptions and system randomness affect realized detection. Text comparisons use the same unwatermarked model, fluency/diversity measures, human judgments, and task-specific correctness such as Pass@k. Image metrics depend on whether watermarking occurs during or after generation.

The agenda seeks application-dependent Pareto improvements across quality, errors, robustness, attribution, payload, and efficiency. It includes advance key commitments against dishonest owners fabricating provenance after seeing content, document-structure watermarks against translation, parameter-embedded watermarks for open models, and cross-modal designs. These are qualified research directions, not established solutions.
attribution_limits: All supplied statements are collaborative. The preferences for accessible formal presentation, low overhead, rigorous evasion evaluation, and Pareto improvement are explicit project-level priorities, not individual preferences attributable to Carlini. Attacks and constructions credited to Saberi et al., Kuditipudi et al., Christ et al., and other cited teams remain those teams’ work. The Gaussian Shading discussion is a survey critique, not a supplied quantitative replication. No individual review-task allocation, reproducible search protocol, or new human-subject study is documented.
tensions_and_counterevidence: The paper calls watermarking useful but incomplete. It criticizes comprehensive logging for storage, coordination, privacy, and open-source limitations, and characterizes passive detection’s empirical error rates and out-of-distribution guarantees as inadequate; these are literature assessments, not implemented comparisons. Its preference for proofs is qualified: empirical validation remains necessary, SynthID is an exception to its small-scale-testing criticism, and heuristic SemStamp/k-SemStamp methods retain research value. Non-robust watermarks can help training-data curation if users lack incentives to evade. Multi-key and multi-sequence verification increases cost and false positives; the surveyed Gumbel construction incurs a factor-L penalty while tolerating edits. Cropping resistance does not imply substitution resistance, and practical PRC-based LLM implementation was still absent in the survey’s timeframe. Text’s lower entropy limits surveyed payloads to a few bits. Publishing keys is described as harmless only for restricted quality/error goals, not adversarial guarantees. Stronger invisibility can enable imperceptible tracking, deanonymization through embedded user IDs, and whistleblower identification. Parameter-based watermarking may complicate key rotation after compromise. Public attribution with strong robustness and practical efficiency remains definition-dependent and unresolved.
coverage_notes: Repeated evidence sets describe one survey, not multiple corroborating projects. The comparison table is qualitative; missing circle encodings prevent recovering individual rankings. Audio/video coverage is comparatively sparse. Policy discussion advocates broad adoption and technically informed international coordination, but does not establish that one unified scheme is the only interoperability route or that Carlini endorses a particular law. The proof-of-generation passage contains an apparent false-positive/false-negative label error; the capsule preserves the substantive post-hoc-key threat rather than that label. Open-source proposals do not establish resistance to arbitrary model modification.

substance:
The project tests whether black-box adversarial-example construction can be recognized from query sequences rather than by judging individual inputs malicious. Defensive success is operationalized as detections—and consequently replacement accounts needed before success—assuming enforceable cancellation and costly account acquisition. The main setting returns categorical labels, not confidence scores.

CIFAR-10 enables broader experimentation than ImageNet; the detector initially wraps a non-robust classifier to isolate its contribution. Raw pixel distance was inadequate because rotations/translations could evade it and storing complete images creates storage and privacy concerns. The replacement is a deliberately simple CNN, initialized from a classifier, with a 256-dimensional output fine-tuned using contrastive loss. Detection uses mean distance to nearest historical encodings. The team selects 50 neighbors where threshold gains plateau, balancing sensitivity against minimum detection delay and computation. Threshold calibration flags 0.1% of randomly streamed training images, not demonstrated real-user traffic.

Randomly targeted attacks receive an L-infinity allowance of 0.05 rather than the roughly 0.031 common in cited white-box evaluations, compensating for black-box difficulty. Trials stop at the first qualifying adversarial example. Unmodified NES and Boundary attacks achieve 100% success while triggering at least 200 detections on average: the claimed benefit is friction, not impossibility.

Adaptive evaluation develops query blinding. A randomized autoencoder uses a substitute classifier trained on 10% of CIFAR-10 rather than the victim; testing distance targets from 2–20 yields a chosen target of 10. NES uses two samples per confidence estimate instead of 50 to reduce detection while remaining reasonably successful. Transformations are normalized to expected pixel-space L2 distortion 2.32, then tested at 5.10. The learned encoder adds little at low distortion but produces 6–8 times more detections than raw distance for tested high-distortion transformations. Candidate-query diversity is improved through graph-based independent-set selection, yielding roughly twice the subset size of greedy selection under simplified assumptions.

Some adaptive changes weaken attacks: brightness blinding corrupts Boundary’s local-geometry estimates, producing overly small steps and premature convergence; larger steps also fail. A hybrid surrogate attack receives otherwise unavailable knowledge of its optimal sampling distance. When random-target attacks fail to find enough target-class samples, evaluation switches to what the paper calls untargeted attacks toward the next-most-likely class, obtaining modest success with fewer detections.

The appendix supplies a substantive limitation: displaced-query, local-linearity estimation lets soft-label NES succeed. Zero-query transfer attacks also bypass monitoring. Adding ensemble adversarial training reduces tested transfer success but increases clean error from 7.8% to 14.6%. Thus results support a conditional hard-label cost-raising defense, not unrestricted black-box robustness.
attribution_limits: The research choices, findings, diagnoses, and realism judgments belong to the Chen–Carlini–Wagner collaboration; no supplied passage assigns their invention or wording to Carlini individually. Experimental measurements concern the stated models and attack implementations. Account economics, buffer strategies, and delayed cancellation are analytical scenarios, not deployment observations. The paper announces source-code release, but the supplied evidence does not independently inspect that code.
tensions_and_counterevidence: Calling hard-label access realistic does not establish that deployed services predominantly use it, and the successful soft-label appendix defeats an unrestricted extension claim. Model secrecy is necessary: extracted weights permit offline attacks that monitoring cannot observe. Protecting a specified input also differs from preventing any error; with the roughly 92%-accurate classifier, the authors estimate about 13 random images could reveal a misclassification under the stated sampling assumption. Calibration on random training images does not establish benign-user false-positive rates, and deployment may require less than 0.1%. Historical economic illustrations estimate more than a year with a 100-hour history or approximately $1,500 to flush a 10,000-query buffer; neither is a current or observed attacker cost. Delayed cancellation could reduce leakage about the encoder but grants additional queries, with one analyzed schedule allowing at most 10% more. Lower-dimensional encodings reduce retention burden without establishing formal privacy.
coverage_notes: Repeated evidence sets are one project. The graph reduction exactly describes a simplified Euclidean detector with k=2, not the full learned k=50 detector. Equal expected pixel distortion does not ensure equal perceptual change or classification preservation. The two-versus-fifty-sample comparison also changes query budgets, and appendix metrics average over successful attacks. The revised hybrid objective is not directly comparable with random-target results. Perlin-noise sampling did not help at the tested larger budgets. Direct evidence remains limited to small-image classification and evaluated attack families; the Dagstuhl discussion is related framing, not a replication.

substance:
The project asks what ordinary API queries reveal about undisclosed production-model internals. Its explicit objective is practical, high-fidelity partial extraction, not bit-for-bit theft of a transformer. Unlike bottom-up approaches, it targets the final projection from a small hidden state into a larger vocabulary-logit space. The threat model excludes timing and implementation side channels.

An explicitly unrealistic full-logit oracle supplies the pedagogical starting point. With sufficiently rich sampled hidden states and a full-rank projection, output vectors reveal hidden dimension through their subspace. Finite precision requires a largest consecutive singular-value-gap criterion rather than exact rank. Across six GPT-2, Pythia, and LLaMA models, five dimension estimates differ by at most one. GPT-2 Small returns 757 rather than 768; inspection of activations from 10,000 queries initially supports that effective rank, but float64 computation reveals all dimensions with much smaller singular values in the remaining directions. Weight validation uses least-squares alignment before RMS comparison, respecting unavoidable transformation ambiguity; random-matrix errors are reported as 100–500 times larger.

Restricted APIs require reconstructing relative logits. A common reference token and four biased tokens exploit top-five log probabilities while respecting softmax’s additive ambiguity. Repeated predictable continuations amortize requests across generated positions. Token expenditure and rate-limited query duration are evaluated separately. A nominally stronger five-logprob variant performs worse because numerical instability requires retries; the measured precision and efficiency advantage selects the four-logprob method. Expensive production-level algorithm ablations are explicitly omitted.

Advance permission determines the five-model OpenAI sample. Detailed results support actual layer extraction for ada and babbage, while GPT-3.5 dimension-only extraction costs under $200. GPT-3.5 widths are provider-confirmed but withheld; several larger full-layer attacks are estimated or unimplemented to preserve weight security. These distinctions narrow broader prose claiming success across all five models. The team reports authorization, provider validation, coordinated mitigation, and notification of potentially affected services.

After disclosure changes prevent logit bias from affecting returned top log probabilities, the authors develop more expensive logprob-free variants that still require bias control. They accumulate inequalities from winning tokens, return feasible bounds at a chosen query budget, accelerate bound computation through shortest paths, and balance returned-token frequencies under a uniform-prior model. Supplementary testing does not establish post-mitigation production extraction.

The work also proves non-identifiability through equivalent parameterizations. Stronger orthogonal-ambiguity recovery is demonstrated only on Pythia-14M because its equation system is prohibitive at production widths. Quantizing Llama-7B to 4 or 8 bits does not hinder tested dimension extraction relative to 16 bits. Recovery remains one-layer-only, with no demonstrated downstream exploitation or immediate practical harm.
attribution_limits: Despite first-author metadata, the motivations, methods, disclosure choices, and normative defense of public vulnerability discussion are collective statements, not separately attributable personal preferences. Open-model weight comparisons, authorized production measurements, provider confirmations, simulated defenses, theoretical proofs, and proposed extensions have different evidentiary status. Withheld GPT-3.5 widths cannot be independently checked from the supplied text. Historical priority and provider-mitigation claims are the paper’s reports, not independently verified current facts.
tensions_and_counterevidence: The detailed implementation table and dimension-only account contradict an expansive reading of prose about all five models: complete larger projection recovery was not demonstrated. The under-$2,000 projection estimate should not erase the separate approximately $8,000 estimate for the chat variant. A broad statement that all attack data were deleted is qualified by an appendix describing retained ada/babbage log probabilities and deleted GPT-3.5 data; exact retention timing remains unresolved. Numerical rank can understate architectural width, and low aligned reconstruction error is not elementwise recovery of original parameters. Near-optimal logprob-free query complexity—approximately one query per logit above a lower bound—is conditional on an acknowledged unrealistic independent uniform prior. Removing useful logit-bias functionality has legitimate-use costs; separating bias from logprob access raises attack cost rather than eliminating all variants. Stateful rate limiting can leak width through its threshold and requires query retention and cross-account coordination with privacy risks. The authors leave incremental hazard beyond ordinary black-box access and approximate distillation unresolved.
coverage_notes: Repeated evidence sets describe one project. Additional diagnostics changed normalization detection below 32-bit precision by mean-centering and controlling intermediate precision; Gopher-7B’s RMSNorm-plus-bias configuration tested a specific confound without a false positive. A restricted top-one-logprob, {-1,0}-bias attack was less numerically stable. Dimension-only extraction can use a vocabulary subset larger than hidden width if rank is retained. A dimensionality-obfuscation example makes GPT-2 Small appear 1,024-dimensional by adding plausible small directions, not a general extraction defense. Prompt-consistent noise was simulated on recovered logits: GPT-2 used true weights as reference, ada/babbage prior extractions; no complete utility-security curve is supplied. The five production targets and prices are historical, and the permission-constrained sample is not provider-representative.

substance:
This collaboration extends an expert-buffer-overflow availability attack into a confidentiality question: can one user's tokens reveal another user's private input through shared mixture-of-experts routing? The investigation assumes white-box access, cross-batch Expert-Choice-Routing, control over relative batch placement, and repeated co-batching with the same victim input. It is explicitly an architectural starting point, not a demonstrated production-service compromise.

The discriminator is a routing tie: a correct token guess can match the victim's routing priority at an expert-capacity boundary, making relative batch order determine which token is processed. Padding enlarges expert capacity; high-affinity blocking sequences leave the desired boundary position available. Implementation inspection prompted padding capacity above 32 to obtain predictable tie handling in the tested PyTorch 2.2.0+cu118 CUDA implementation. Blocker construction uses 9,218 prefix-free tokens from Mixtral's 32,000-token vocabulary and a 0.85 priority threshold, avoiding accidental token merging during concatenation.

Changed outputs alone were insufficient evidence: numerical instability, suffix-induced prefix dropping, and simultaneous dropout could create false positives. The authors therefore estimated prefix routing, cached attention activations, selectively disabled local experts, and mapped outputs to routing paths. Approximate nearest-neighbor matching using the stated L0 metric accommodated floating-point discrepancies. Evaluation shortcuts restricted paths to within four bits of an estimate and skipped enumeration when paired logits were sufficiently close. A separate oracle verifies a completely specified candidate prompt through its last token with two target queries; this is not two-query recovery of an unknown prompt.

Experiments used only Mixtral-8x7B's first two transformer blocks, replaced its router with ECR, restricted guesses to 27 lowercase-letter/space tokens, and deliberately induced ties through five-digit rounding. Across 1,000 common English words, eight experts, and six padding lengths, recovery reached 996 complete messages and 4,833 of 4,838 tokens. Extraction advanced after any expert succeeded; additional experts had diminishing returns but were needed to exceed 99% success. Padding length 40 worked best locally: larger buffers reduce incidental dropping but demand longer blockers whose unwanted tokens can disrupt routing.

Remote complexity is O(VM²), versus O(2^(DN)VM²) local queries, with vocabulary size V, message length M, depth D, and expert count N. Approximately 100 remote queries per token therefore understates total work. The authors call the current attack infeasible against real-world systems. Learned routing inference, final-layer targeting, improved guessing, and black-box variants remain proposals. Preserving cross-user batch independence and introducing stochasticity are proposed defenses, not measured protections; the broader conclusion concerns interactions among architecture, implementation, and serving.
attribution_limits: All research choices, results, recommendations, and prospective beliefs are attributed to the collaboration. No supplied statement individually identifies Nicholas Carlini as originating the attack, making an implementation decision, or expressing a personal preference. Metadata lists him last but author position and date are not independently verified. Experimental results are author-reported; proposed scalability improvements and defenses must not be presented as completed research or deployed protections.
tensions_and_counterevidence: The broad disclosure language is qualified by four incompletely recovered messages, five unrecovered tokens, an assisted two-block experiment, and attacker capabilities the authors themselves characterize as unrealistic. Naturally occurring tie prevalence is not established. The main text describes rounding router weights, Appendix A describes attention outputs, and the code rounds routing weights; Appendix D also contains inconsistent threshold wording. CUDA behavior depends on implementation, size, and options and does not transfer automatically to CPU. The output-closeness shortcut has no supplied threshold or independently quantified false-negative rate, and approximate routing matching lacks a general error bound. First-success expert plots depend on search order, not independent measurements of every expert's leakage potential. Randomization is not tested against adaptive repeated-query attacks.
coverage_notes: Numerous evidence records repeat the same passages and decisions; they represent one project, not independent corroboration. The distinction between the 27-token extraction vocabulary and the much larger blocker-construction vocabulary is essential. Reproducibility provisions include the open base model, algorithm descriptions, figures, hyperparameters, router code, slicing, and loading hooks, but no independent replication is documented. The demonstrated capacity optimum and routing heuristics are setup-specific, not general researcher preferences or universal attack parameters.

substance:
The collaboration asks whether distillation's indirect access to teacher training data actually protects membership privacy. Because distillation alone lacks a rigorous privacy guarantee, it selects empirical membership inference, citing that attack's established research base. Scope deliberately excludes attacks on composite ensemble or differentially private systems. Three settings separate private teacher data, private student data, and self-distillation with identical datasets.

Experiments span CIFAR-10, WikiText103, Purchase100, and Texas100. CIFAR-10 preprocessing removes 5,275 duplicates and creates teacher/student sets of 30,000/14,725 examples. Fast DAWNBench ResNet-9 code is adapted for distillation and LiRA subsampling. Default calibration uses 100 shadow models, with figures evaluated over more than 1,000 models. Reporting uses per-example membership accuracy for one or two attacks and ROC curves for larger comparisons, preserving heterogeneous vulnerability rather than relying exclusively on averages.

Transfer LiRA calibrates on shadow teachers without performing distillation, then applies the test to students. End-to-End LiRA instead reproduces teacher training and distillation, calibrating on shadow students; its stronger pipeline match requires knowledge of the student training set. Average attack accuracy and low-FPR performance decrease after distillation, but 5% of examples lose fewer than eight percentage points of vulnerability on CIFAR-10, five on Purchase100, and four on Texas100. The paper consequently judges protection limited under its worst-case-oriented privacy standard, while acknowledging substantial benefits for some examples.

To locate the information pathway, a new attack uses only teacher responses on student queries, not predictions on target teacher examples. A poor initial adaptation prompted two repairs: model the target teacher-label logit rather than the student-label logit, and retain queries with the largest absolute IN/OUT mean-logit differences. Ablations compare both choices; the unmodified attack is at chance, while both modifications with ten selected queries achieve TPR 10^-3 at FPR 10^-4 on CIFAR-10. This expensive investigation uses 4,000 shadow models and excludes WikiText103.

Reintroducing removed CIFAR-10 near-duplicates increases leakage, with a reported Chow-test p-value below 10^-15; deduplication reduces rather than eliminates indirect leakage. Label-flipping poisoning increases teacher vulnerability without visibly changing its relationship to student vulnerability. Student-targeted poisoning remains open. Lower distillation temperatures mildly reduce observed student leakage, contrary to prior work, and the authors cannot reverse that benefit with their attacks.

For private student data, exact-teacher, candidate-set, and surrogate-teacher settings vary attacker knowledge. Even the surrogate reaches TPR 10^-2 at FPR 10^-3 on CIFAR-10. Self-distillation experiments reproduce the full algorithm and find a small apparent attack increase with greater distillation-loss weighting. Practical guidance treats differential privacy as complementary and rejects assuming student data becomes private merely through distillation.
attribution_limits: The evidence documents collaborative experimental choices and interpretations, not individually attributable Carlini speech or private preferences. Metadata lists him last, without independently verified contribution assignments. The logit-coordinate change is a documented attack-development revision within this project, not a change in his general research views. Membership-inference success, compute costs, and uncertainty estimates are reported experimental data; interpolation, reinforced memorization, explanations of prior temperature results, and student-targeted poisoning are interpretations or proposed research rather than established mechanisms.
tensions_and_counterevidence: Distillation does provide average and example-specific privacy benefits; the paper's unfavorable overall assessment depends on persistently vulnerable examples and its worst-case evaluative standard, not a universal impossibility theorem. Estimated coordinate standard deviations of about 1.5 percentage points separate some sampling uncertainty from genuine heterogeneity. Attacks on trained students outperform the implemented query-only attack even though students post-process those queries: the proposed interpolation explanation concerns accessibility of existing information, not creation of extra information. Temperature tests from 0.1 to 4 retain similar model accuracy and show roughly a fourfold TPR reduction at FPR 10^-3 between extremes. The proposed explanation for disagreement with earlier high-temperature findings is hypothetical. Scaling can be undone on exposed query logits, but student-logit rescaling does not remove the observed benefit because LiRA is scale-invariant; failure to find an adaptive reversal is not a privacy guarantee. Reduced teacher knowledge weakens private-student attacks, and the self-distillation effect is small.
coverage_notes: Repeated records are consolidated into one study. Dataset breadth does not imply every attack was tested on every dataset: the query-only language-model experiment was omitted for cost. Fast implementations reportedly enabled fewer than 30,000 CIFAR-10 models in under one GPU-week, using four GPUs to reduce wall-clock time. The authors state, 'Unfortunately, we are unable to make our code public at this time due to organizational constraints.' The organization, Carlini's role in that restriction, and any later release are unspecified; this is a reproducibility limitation, not evidence of opposition to code sharing. Deliberate duplicate reintroduction is an experimental intervention, not abandonment of deduplication guidance.

substance:
Terminal-Bench addresses a claimed gap between realistic professional work and tasks difficult enough to distinguish frontier agents. Its 2.0 dataset selects 89 of 229 tasks from 93 contributors, covering legacy-system configuration, research-paper reimplementation, and software engineering. Success tests inspect final container state rather than command sequences or console output; the benchmark permits tools beyond terminals, although individual tasks can impose explicit constraints.

Construction separates specificity, solvability, and integrity. Instructions and tests should agree bidirectionally on acceptable states; executable oracle workflows demonstrate solvability; unavailable-in-deployment shortcuts, such as future Git commits, should be removed. Admission checks require oracle success and no-op-agent failure. Human-written specifications and minimally model-assisted oracle solutions are requested through contributor attestations. Deterministic and LLM-backed checks precede roughly three reviewer-hours per task. Reviewers diagnose whether failed runs indicate capability limits or defective tasks rather than equating failure with difficulty. Oracle checks distinguish deriving an answer from simply writing a known result.

Adversarial auditing uses an OpenHands exploit agent without access to tests or oracle solutions, followed by human inspection regardless of success. It finds monkey-patching, guessing, and enumerating every answer to exploit tests checking only for correct-answer presence. Tests, solutions, and test dependencies are kept out of initial agent images.

Terminus 2 supplies a minimal headless-terminal/Bash scaffold to reduce scaffold-specific bias. Supported model-agent combinations receive at least five runs, totaling 32,155 task attempts. Configurable reasoning uses provider defaults. Headline plots select each model's best tested scaffold and show 95% confidence intervals; they are not fixed-scaffold comparisons. Harbor supplies reusable execution infrastructure. External-benchmark adapters require natural-language tasks, containers, and programmatic evaluation, with repeated same-model/same-agent parity checks before integration; reference solutions are optional for adapters.

Failure analysis samples two failed Terminus 2 trials per model per task. The taxonomy is adapted to single-agent affordances, excluding unavailable clarification and using separate rubrics for distinct failure modes. Docent-assisted exploration and two human annotators refine labels. GPT-5 trajectory judgments report 90% agreement, 92% precision, and 90% recall against 120 human-labeled traces. Command-error detection separately reports 92.4% agreement on 66 pairs; classification reports 82% against 50 author annotations. Among 3,800 sampled command failures, missing executables/PATH problems account for 24.1%, followed by execution failures at 9.6%.

Average turns show essentially no success correlation, and higher token use does not necessarily predict better performance. Human-medium/model-hard disagreements include XSS-filter bypasses and Redcode strategy; the interpretation invokes creative/adversarial reasoning, not an isolated causal result. Proposed improvements depend on failure profiles. The authors explicitly accept greater verification difficulty for crowdsourced diversity and realism, recommend substantial manual auditing, and plan harder task sets as models improve.
attribution_limits: This is a large collaborative project; no supplied evidence assigns particular tasks, reviews, annotations, infrastructure, or wording to Carlini. Metadata places him within the author list but does not establish contributions and is not independently verified. First-person checklist text is a contributor template, not personal testimony. Rubric thresholds classify evaluated agents and must not become claims about Carlini's own debugging, stopping, communication, or verification habits. Manual-audit recommendations and the diversity-versus-verifiability tradeoff are explicit collective positions. Model-judge agreement is author-reported validation, not independent certification.
tensions_and_counterevidence: Internet access supports realistic installation and research but permits discovery of public oracle solutions; non-observation across tens of thousands of trajectories is not protection. Canary strings are described as largely symbolic, unselected tasks remain public, and a genuinely private set is deferred because of construction costs. Containers, bundled dependencies, and pinning do not eliminate external-resource, hardware, API, or infrastructure nondeterminism. Python dependencies are pinned, but apt versions deliberately are not because old versions can disappear. The checklist acknowledges missing objective automated test-quality metrics and no quantitative estimate of how residual exploits, underspecification, or solvability flaws affect scores. Checklist authors participated in development, so their involvement is not wholly detached validation. Human difficulty ratings are estimates rather than measured completion times; empirical difficulty depends on selected models and scaffold. Failure-conditioned samples, small judge-validation sets, and non-fully-crossed model/scaffold compatibility limit generalization. More turns or tokens lacking aggregate correlation does not show extra inference effort cannot help. Suggested interventions, saturation forecasts, and future releases are not completed results.
coverage_notes: Repeated passages describe one benchmark project. Supplied evidence flags inconsistent task/model counts elsewhere; the capsule retains the explicitly reported 89 selected tasks and 32,155 trials without reconstructing missing totals. Detailed rubrics provide operational nuance: fully corrected violations are excluded; substitutions need demonstrated equivalence; examples are not binding requirements unless specified; repetition is counted per tool-call block and requires substantive rather than cosmetic change. Stopping labels allow one post-success verification turn and flag continued identical approaches after two consecutive failures, with meaningful strategy changes resetting the counter. Context loss requires contradiction of established state or commitments; involuntary endings and actionable incomplete handoffs are distinguished from premature completion. Verification requires observed core-property evidence, can flag bypassed designated verifiers, and distinguishes weak checking from fabricated evidence. Claims are judged against contemporaneous evidence; authoritative evaluators or explicitly narrowed claims can justify bounded checking. These are annotation definitions, not evidence of researcher conduct. One supplied note reports a cutoff before the complete Weak Verification procedure, and adapter-specific parity outcomes are unavailable.

substance:
In this February 2025 interview, Carlini distinguishes attack feasibility, real-world exposure, and privacy research from refuting particular defenses: he says only two or three recent papers did the latter. He enjoys attacking image defenses but acknowledges selecting unusual proposals he suspects are weak, inflating apparent success. He aims to reserve at least half his time for technically driven papers while advising others through meetings, experimental direction, and writing.

His optimization framework separates objective from optimizer, excluding conversational social engineering. Simple, debuggable losses generally outweigh elegance or marginal gains; he endorses simpler PGD over his earlier elaborate formulation. Yet inexpensive image evaluations merit roughly 1,000 iterations to avoid false robustness from underoptimization. Diagnosis targets mechanisms rather than defense narratives: softmax saturation in distillation can suppress gradients, while float64 or logit rescaling restores them; straight-through estimators address some discontinuities. TAR reminded him of weak one-step adversarial training defeated by iterative attacks. Students’ fine-tuning-resistance attacks adapted this history through learning-rate changes, restarts, and warmups; he disclaims their technical implementation.

The suffix collaboration optimized an affirmative opening rather than an unknown complete answer, using gradients to suggest token substitutions and checking actual replacements with substantial search compute. The proxy can fail under defenses that decouple affirmation from compliance. One recalled suffix produced toxic content followed by a compliment, suggesting—but not mechanistically establishing—partly interpretable features. Poisoning examples contrast a few hundred mislabeled images in internet-trained image systems with language-model attacks needing persistence through SFT/RLHF. He flags 0.1% of a trillion tokens as a billion-token burden; lower-budget poisoning remains conjectural.

Privacy measurement requires distinguishing document frequency, within-document repetition, and epochs; later closed production models prevent his GPT-2-style exposure accounting. Diffusion extraction varied from success around 100 repetitions to failure around 10,000, without an explanation. Fact editing is not robust knowledge removal: subsequent fine-tuning or in-context learning might recover capabilities. Those recovery scenarios are hypotheses, not reported tests; he tentatively favors informed refusal while advocating experiments on competing approaches.

Reported automation experiments found models could attack defenses reduced to 20 Python lines but failed on original repositories, motivating end-to-end evaluation of finding the consequential mechanism. He also values bounded proxy problems when their limits stay explicit. His deployment forecast favors containing persistent model errors: an external password-field prohibition illustrates protection with utility costs and JavaScript coverage gaps. He supports independent red teams, layered detectors, and limited proof-of-concept disclosure, not prolonged weaponization. Present-day open-source support is explicit but revisable; policy should use accurate technical premises rather than assume unavailable lockdown.
attribution_limits: This is multi-speaker interview material, despite solo-author metadata. Preferences, heuristics, and forecasts above are Carlini’s explicit statements; neither the interviewer’s publication-count superlative nor reported challenge outcomes are independently established. Carlini describes the suffix and language-model poisoning projects as mainly advisory and explicitly assigns fine-tuning-resistance implementation to students. Extraction and automation findings are collaborative, retrospectively reported results without full experimental protocols here. The geometric poisoning construction, unlearning paper, earlier independent-direction results, and obfuscated-activation work discussed belong to other researchers. Architectural examples, capability-recovery scenarios, and future release thresholds are proposals or hypotheticals, not demonstrated systems. His half-time allocation is an intention, not audited time use.
tensions_and_counterevidence: He generally declines to attack incremental adversarial-training variants because he trusts their foundation; his successes therefore do not imply universal defensive failure. Roughly 70% accuracy under attack can represent major scientific progress without meeting a repeated-adversary security standard. His five-to-ten-idea exhaustion heuristic is not a robustness certificate. Visual intuition guides exploration, but he qualifies misleading high-dimensional geometry claims and returns to numerical execution; he explicitly prefers empirical evidence over speculative brain analogies. Human-written jailbreaks outperform the optimization attacks he expected to be stronger, an unresolved discrepancy. Attackers moving second have an advantage, but internet poisoning can reverse move order. Failed image extraction does not prove absence of memorization. He accepts partial interpretability and potentially unexplained empirical robustness, rather than demanding complete mechanistic explanations. Layered detectors may fail together; excessive warnings can destroy useful signals, and manipulation resistance can conflict with accepting legitimate corrections. His open-source default confronts concentrated-power risks on one side and hypothetical broadly capable offensive systems on the other; he leaves both release and attack-research choices revisable. Cryptographic weak breaks matter as early warnings, despite his different practical stopping threshold for marginal ML attack improvements.
coverage_notes: Numerous evidence records repeat the same interview passages, often three times; they are one source, not independent corroboration. Several distinct projects are recalled without their underlying papers, code, model lists, or sample sizes. Conversational percentages, dates, and attack-direction counts are approximate. One record says the supplied source ends during the jailbreak-challenge exchange, while other supplied records contain later exchanges; this inconsistency does not justify discarding those records or reconstructing missing text. Metadata dates and authorship positions are unverified. His historical analogies changed expectations about repeated latent-defense bypasses, but do not establish equivalence between image and language-model mechanisms.

substance:
The study asks whether 12 jailbreak and prompt-injection defenses survive defense-aware attackers with substantial resources, not how cheaply they can be defeated. It adapts existing gradient, reinforcement-learning, search, and human techniques within a propose–score–select–update framework. Each defense receives a likely-effective attack rather than an exhaustive attack cross-product; original evaluation protocols are retained, so results across HarmBench, AgentDojo, OpenPromptInject, and adversarial Davinci are not a common ranking.

Carlini’s credited gradient experiments follow GCG, use negative model loss, and target only RPO: reported success is 96%, versus 98% for RL under the original HarmBench protocol. RL uses five feedback-driven attempts per session, the best session score, 32 independent sessions per sample, and GRPO policy updates with an unnamed unaligned closed-source model. Rewards and supplied defense-methodology descriptions are defense-specific.

Search separates controller, mutator, and scorer. After limited comparison with a single-database evolutionary algorithm, the team adopts Island/MAP Elites without subsequent hyperparameter tuning, retaining candidates by length and diversity. Gemini-2.5 Pro at maximum thinking budget proposes eight candidates per iteration. Victim outputs and a critic’s 1–10 score provide progress signals because binary success is too sparse and ordinary log-probability was judged unhelpful. Changing histories occupy user messages while fixed system prompts are cached to reduce cost.

Concrete findings include prompting defenses with static success as low as 1% but adaptive success above 95% in highlighted settings, not every model pairing. MetaSecAlign moves from reported 2% static success to 96% adaptive success. Giving the MELON attacker implementation knowledge raises success from 76% to 95%. Data Sentinel attacks substitute spam classification for sentiment analysis, or conversely, with over 80% replacement-task accuracy and detector bypass; unchanged output structure masks semantic task redefinition.

Evaluation includes 80 AgentDojo samples from Slack, Travel, and Workspace, omitting Banking as less realistic in the authors’ judgment. Crucially, plan-then-execute defenses are excluded because data-independent planning prevents attacks in most selected scenarios. Legitimate-task utility is measured on all AgentDojo scenarios; filtering defenses substantially reduce it, while acceptable-false-positive recalibration remains untested.

A 40-challenge, $20,000 human competition supplies live execution feedback, rewards shorter successes, and adjudicates scoring appeals. Main-paper comparisons count attacker-task success alone, unlike the competition’s requirement that both tasks succeed. Across 29 overlapping scenarios, collective humans achieve 100% versus search’s 69% at 800 queries, but this compares many independent people with one search run. Manual verification is reported, yet StruQ experiments expose repetition-based reward hacking whose full correction is not documented.
attribution_limits: An explicit contribution statement jointly credits Carlini and Milad Nasr with proposing RL-based adaptive attacks and initial development, while acknowledging independent similar suggestions by Jamie Hayes, Chawin Sitawarin, and Juliette Pluto. Carlini is specifically credited with gradient work, gradient experiments, initial drafting, and his attack section. Nasr implemented and ran RL; Sitawarin implemented search; other collaborators organized the human study. Thus search architecture, competition incentives, ethics procedures, and general recommendations are collective evidence, not Carlini’s personal preferences. The reported informed participation, anonymization, avoidance of sensitive personal data, and provider notification likewise cannot be assigned to him individually. Publication’s claimed net safety benefit is the authors’ ethical judgment, not a measured outcome.
tensions_and_counterevidence: Despite Carlini’s gradient contribution, the paper recommends direct text-space methods because current gradient attacks are unreliable; this does not establish his personal reversal. GPT-5 Mini and some PIGuard combinations resist search more strongly. Search often plateaus after 100–200 queries; improved success through parallel trials is conjectural, not demonstrated. The best of three humans covering every comparison scenario achieves 75%, while search outperforms the other two; unequal effort and independent attempts prevent a normalized human–automation ranking. Human competition participants were blinded to defenses, weaker information access than the defense-informed red-teaming the paper recommends. Query medians exclude unsuccessful 800-query searches, and Protect AI excludes tasks whose secrets were redacted, changing its denominator. Detector prose says greater than 90% for three systems, but the table gives exactly 90% for Protect AI and Model Armor with Gemini-2.5 Pro. Manual verification lacks a supplied rubric; StruQ repetition shows that high proxy scores need not establish substantive compromise. Excluded plan-then-execute architectures are acknowledged counterexamples within many selected scenarios, although their utility limitations are asserted without quantified evaluation here. Detectors retain a proposed limited role against opportunistic attacks despite adaptive failures.
coverage_notes: The packet repeatedly supplies overlapping versions of the same paper passages; count this as one collaborative project. Main and appendix results use different success units: submission-level competition ASR, attacker-only outcomes, and collective scenario-level success are not interchangeable. Appendix RL scoring mentions MetaSecAlign although the main mapping assigns it search and human attacks; no additional RL result should be inferred. The rendered MELON payload and illustrative appendix triggers are unavailable, so their contents cannot be reconstructed. Illustrative triggers were selected by scenario order conditional on success, not randomly. Familiar encodings, languages, structured formats, and disguises emerged, but the authors’ claim of no wholly new strategy is only an informal inspection. Robustness conclusions cover the evaluated defenses and threat models, not all architectural defenses or practical attack costs.

substance:
The Equational Theories Project deliberately chose a mathematically substantive universal-algebra classification suited to distributed, computer-assisted research: determine implications among 4,694 magma laws of order at most four. It subsequently added the finite-magma graph. The unrestricted classification was completed, but E677 implying E255 over finite magmas remained open up to duality; an infinite counterexample did not resolve it.

Research moved from broad inexpensive methods toward specialized constructions. Enumeration through size four reportedly refuted 13,632,566 implications using 524 magmas and 165 CPU-hours. Unstructured size-five sampling added little because those magmas satisfied few new laws; linear, quadratic, and cancellative families were more productive, whereas commutative examples contributed little. Formalization costs influenced mathematical presentation: a shift-operator counterexample became the integer operation 2x minus floor(y/2), and some SAT-generated greedy-construction rules were replaced by shorter human versions. Greedy construction iteratively repaired collisions, but rule discovery had no termination guarantee. Randomized finite-model transformations needed no independent correctness proof because successful candidates could be checked directly.

Implementation separated a custom Magma operation from existing multiplication, and maintained semantic EquationX representations for individual implications alongside syntactic LawX representations for metatheorems. External ATP scripts generated persistent Lean source because this was quick to implement and imposed little contributor setup. Certificates were reconstructed rather than trusting prover verdicts. Extensions such as duper and egg stayed outside the master repository, sometimes requiring manual translation. Axiom checking and exclusion of native_decide narrowed the trusted base. For feasible compilation, Lean verified a generating set of 10,657 positive and 586,925 negative implications; external programs performed graph closure, rather than one end-to-end Lean theorem.

Coordination combined Zulip discussion, exclusive task claims, pull-request review, CI checks, and accessible graph interfaces. Since proofs were being discovered, the blueprint evolved rather than preceding implementation. Early maintenance weaknesses produced duplicated free-magma infrastructure that the team later judged too costly to replace, motivating a recommendation to appoint maintainers before launch.

Solver engineering was problem-dependent. For E1518, combining two valid injectivity conditions worsened performance, so only the better-performing condition was retained. Left-inverse encodings generally helped Prover9–Mace4 but slightly hurt Vampire. Problem-specific isomorphism discriminators reportedly reduced one computation from ten days to 0.02 seconds.

LLMs helped interfaces and completion, and ChatGPT proposed a subsequently verified E3523 rewriting system, but usually added little on resistant implications. A five-layer character-level CNN achieved 99.7% accuracy; random labels yielded 49.99%, and 5% training data retained 99.6%. These controls did not settle whether it learned equation structure or graph regularities; proposed random-poset controls and higher-order search guidance remained untested.
attribution_limits: All supplied substantive statements concern collective work, not individually attributed statements or personal preferences of Nicholas Carlini. Coauthorship does not identify who selected the problem, implemented tools, designed the CNN, used LLMs, or made specification mistakes. Activity logging is attributed to the main organizer, not specifically Carlini. Recommendations are collective retrospective judgments; numerical performance results are reported experiments. Metadata positions and dates were not independently verified.
tensions_and_counterevidence: Formal checking did not remove specification or infrastructure risks: human review remained necessary, CI and extraction scripts were unverified, and quantifier-scope errors produced false apparent proofs of the open finite implication. The authors explicitly offered an informal ATP field report, not a calibrated benchmark, citing missing benchmarking expertise. Solver rankings could reverse with model size; finding one model and exhausting a size required different configurations, and ATP failure supplied only heuristic compatibility evidence. The enumeration record's reported 96.3% share of false implications conflicts with another total and should not be endorsed. Weak central groupoid orders n² or 2n² were empirical, unproved observations. CNN accuracy excluded 362 unresolved hard cases; its approximate 700 kB representation was larger than the exact compressed 40 kB bit table.
coverage_notes: Numerous records repeat the same passages and decisions; they are not independent support. Additional distinctive work includes the months-long, over-4,000-line E1729 refutation, squares-first constructions, twisting a five-coordinate NAND magma, and solver-assisted evolution of E854 models seeded with E10 violations. Spectrum work proved full spectrum for 3,074 remaining laws using 3,068 linear constructions plus six special cases. The Higman–Neumann investigation filtered 298,012,537 laws before ATP search and reported 179 unrestricted characterizations, 21 finite characterizations with unresolved infinite status, and 13 unresolved candidates. Its blanket statement that results were not yet Lean-formalized coexists with reports that some component proofs were ported; neither should erase the other.

substance:
This project asks whether removing especially memorized examples can substantially protect the remaining dataset without requiring uniform, algorithm-level privacy guarantees.
